n:
- The word *revelation* (Greek *apokalupsis*) introduces the book's visionary style as apocalyptic writing (see Revelation Book Introduction, “Apocalyptic Writing”). God shares his message through mysterious symbols, numbers, and word pictures. 

- *of Jesus Christ*: He is both the source and the main subject of the book. 

- *what must soon come to pass*: Compare {{Revelation 3:11|Revelation 3:11}}; {{Revelation 22:6-7|22:6–7}}; {{Luke 18:8|Luke 18:8}}; {{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}.

Revelation is a letter to the believers in seven churches in Asia Minor. The letter is full of prophecy. It’s known as apocalyptic writing.

John began the letter by praising God the Father. He also praised Jesus Christ the Messiah. Jesus has authority over all rulers on earth.

John reminded the believers of many things that were true about them. They served the King who has all glory and power. The believers were loved by Jesus. They were part of the kingdom of God and part of God’s family. Because of this they were royal and were priests.

This was like what God called his people from the nation of Israel. Long ago God called them a kingdom of priests.

John used words from prophets in the Old Testament. He used them to talk about Jesus’ return in the future. Jesus described himself as the Alpha and the Omega. He promised to come back to earth.

Revelation begins with a three-part introduction, including: 

- a prologue ({{Revelation 1:1-3|Revelation 1:1–3}}), 

- a letter introduction ({{Revelation 1:4-8|Revelation 1:4–8}}), and

- a historical introduction ({{Revelation 1:9-11|Revelation 1:9–11}}).

*testifies* … *testimony*: The Greek words behind these terms are *martureō* (meaning “to bear witness”) and *marturia* (meaning “witness” or “testimony”). These related Greek words refer to a true and reliable witness. They highlight that the sacrificial witness of Jesus and the true testimony of John form the foundation for the revelation.

- *blessed is the one*: Revelation includes seven promises of blessing ({{Revelation 1:3|Revelation 1:3}}; {{Revelation 14:13|14:13}}; {{Revelation 16:15|16:15}}; {{Revelation 19:9|19:9}}; {{Revelation 20:6|20:6}}; {{Revelation 22:7|22:7}}, {{Revelation 22:14|14}}). 

- *hear and obey*: True listening means you follow what you hear.

- *To the seven churches* do not mean there were only seven churches in the Roman province of Asia. Instead, these seven churches represent the entire group. "Grace and peace" is a typical Christian greeting (see study notes on 2 Corinthians 1:1–2; 2 Thessalonians 1:1–2). The order of these words is consistent in the New Testament, suggesting that peace follows from God's grace. 

- *from Him who is and was and is to come*: God controlled the past, will control the future, and has complete authority and power over every present crisis (see also {{Revelation 1:8|Revelation 1:8}}; {{Revelation 4:8|4:8}}; {{Revelation 11:17|11:17}}; {{Revelation 16:5|16:5}}). 

- *the seven spirits*: Some argue that the "seven spirits" are seven angels, but the phrase fits between references to God the Father ({{Revelation 1:4|Revelation 1:4}}) and God the Son ({{Revelation 1:5|1:5}}), making this passage a description of the Trinity (see {{Matthew 28:19|Matthew 28:19}}; {{John 14:26|John 14:26}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:14|2 Corinthians 13:14}}; {{1 Peter 1:2|1 Peter 1:2}}). The number seven acknowledges the holy spirit’s perfection (compare {{Zechariah 4:2|Zechariah 4:2}}, {{Zechariah 4:6|6}}, {{Zechariah 4:10|10}}).
The second introduction (see study note on Revelation 1:1–11) follows the style of a Greek letter.

- Jesus serves as our example for sharing the good of salvation ({{Revelation 1:2|Revelation 1:2}}). 

- The belief that Jesus was the first to rise from the dead is essential to Christian faith ({{1 Corinthians 15:14|1 Corinthians 15:14}}, {{1 Corinthians 15:17|17}}). 

- As the ruler of all the kings of the world (see also {{Revelation 17:14|Revelation 17:14}}; {{Revelation 19:16|19:16}}), he is the ultimate Lord of everything. People in the Roman world were expected to declare Caesar as the absolute lord; many early Christians died for their belief that Jesus alone holds that position.

- In this doxology, John explains why we should praise Jesus.

- A doxology is a short statement that gives praise to God or to Jesus. These statements often end with the word *Amen* (see {{Romans 11:36|Romans 11:36}}; {{Philippians 4:20|Philippians 4:20}}), which expresses agreement and affirmation.

*I am* is the name of God in the Old Testament ({{Exodus 3:13-14|Exodus 3:13–14}}; {{Exodus 6:2|6:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:4|Deuteronomy 6:4}}). Jesus used this name for himself (compare {{John 4:26|John 4:26}}). Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. They show that God's actions cover everything. God is completely in control.

- *your brother and partner*: Although separated from other Christians due to imprisonment, John felt a sense of community with them in suffering. This connection was based on hope in God's kingdom and a willingness to endure. 

- The Roman fortress on the island of Patmos held prisoners and exiles. Patmos was part of a group of islands that protected the busy seaport of Miletus. 

- *because of the word of God and my testimony*: These two statements mean the same thing. This is a common pattern in Semitic writing, where the second line repeats or explains the first. By John's time, Jews were convincing Roman authorities that Christianity was different from Judaism and therefore not an authorized religion.
This third introduction (see study note on Revelation 1:1–11) is historical. It shows God speaking to people through real events. While in exile, God gave John an important mission.

Both John and the believers he wrote to were suffering. They were being treated badly for following Jesus as Lord.

The first vision John wrote about occurred on Patmos on the Lord’s day. The vision was of Jesus after his resurrection from the dead.

Jesus looked to John like the son of man and the Eternal God. The prophet Daniel had talked about them in a vision recorded in Daniel 7:9–22.

The words that Jesus spoke looked to John like a sword. In the book of Isaiah the words of God’s servant were also like a sword (Isaiah 49:2).

The vision of Jesus was so powerful that John felt as if he had died. But Jesus comforted John. He wanted John to share his message with the churches. The seven lampstands were a sign of the churches.

- *the Lord’s day*: In the Roman world, this term referred to celebrations for Caesar. Christians, however, used it for their weekly worship, celebrating the resurrection of Jesus. The earliest Christians worshiped in Jewish synagogues on the Sabbath, the last day of the week ({{Acts 18:4|Acts 18:4}}). By the time of Revelation, they were no longer allowed in synagogues and gathered on the first day of the week, which marked the resurrection (see study note on Luke 24:1; see also {{Acts 20:7|Acts 20:7}}). 

- The loud voice like a trumpet blast announced the Lord’s coming.

*Write … and send*: God appointed John as a prophet and messenger of his revelation (see {{Revelation 22:8|Revelation 22:8}}, {{Revelation 22:10|10}}; compare {{Isaiah 6:8-9|Isaiah 6:8–9}}; {{Jeremiah 2:1-2|Jeremiah 2:1–2}}; {{Ezekiel 2:1-3|Ezekiel 2:1–3}}; {{Ezekiel 34:1-2|34:1–2}}).

- *I turned to see the voice that was speaking*: This refers to the loud voice in {{Revelation 1:10|Revelation 1:10}}.

- *seven gold lampstands*: The lighted menorah was a symbol of God's presence among his people ({{Exodus 27:21|Exodus 27:21}}; {{Leviticus 24:1-4|Leviticus 24:1–4}}) and his all-seeing eyes in the world ({{Zechariah 4:10|Zechariah 4:10}}).
John's first vision shows Christ as a wise, strong, and powerful messenger of God who always cares for his people.

- *the Son of Man* (or *a son of man*): *Son of Man* is a title Jesus used for himself (see {{Daniel 7:13|Daniel 7:13}}; {{Matthew 8:20|Matthew 8:20}}; {{Matthew 9:6|9:6}}; {{Matthew 16:13|16:13}}; {{Mark 2:28|Mark 2:28}}; {{Mark 9:9|9:9}}; {{Mark 14:41|14:41}}; {{John 1:51|John 1:51}}; {{John 3:13|3:13}}; {{John 5:27|5:27}}). 

- The long robe and gold sash give Christ an authoritative look (see {{Revelation 19:13-16|Revelation 19:13–16}}; {{Daniel 10:5|Daniel 10:5}}). The robe was a priestly garment symbolizing purity and holiness.

- White hair symbolizes wisdom and maturity. This image reflects Daniel’s vision of the Ancient One ({{Daniel 7:9|Daniel 7:9}}). 

- His eyes, like flames of fire, see through deception. The one who knows everything will judge everyone (see {{Daniel 10:6|Daniel 10:6}}; {{Hebrews 4:13|Hebrews 4:13}}).

- Refined or hardened bronze feet suggest stability, firmness, and security (compare {{Daniel 10:6|Daniel 10:6}}). 

- The thundering voice shows God's power. When God speaks, people will listen (compare {{Ezekiel 43:2|Ezekiel 43:2}}).

- The seven stars symbolize the complete church. The church is safe in the right hand of the Son of Man, which means it is under his care, acceptance, and blessing. 

- The sharp sword coming from his mouth represents his powerful message and judgment (see {{Revelation 19:15|Revelation 19:15}}; {{Genesis 3:24|Genesis 3:24}}; {{Ephesians 6:17|Ephesians 6:17}}; {{Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12}}). Jesus announces both grace and judgment, but here the focus is on his role in carrying out judgment (see {{Revelation 2:12|Revelation 2:12}}, {{Revelation 2:16|16}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}, {{Revelation 19:21|21}}; compare {{Isaiah 11:4|Isaiah 11:4}}).

- *When I saw Him, I fell … dead*: Terror and fainting, if not death itself (see {{Exodus 33:20|Exodus 33:20}}), often occur when someone sees God (see {{Isaiah 6:1-5|Isaiah 6:1–5}}; {{Matthew 28:4|Matthew 28:4}}). The Lord kindly responds by touching with his right hand (compare {{Matthew 25:34|Matthew 25:34}}) and saying, *Do not be afraid* (compare {{Luke 1:13|Luke 1:13}}), showing both grace and acceptance. 

- *I am*: This phrase identifies Jesus as God (see study note on Revelation 1:8).

- *the Living One*: The Son of Man ({{Revelation 1:13|Revelation:13}}) has defeated death, so he holds the keys to death and controls the outcome of our greatest fear (see {{Revelation 20:14|Revelation 20:14}}; {{Hebrews 2:14-15|Hebrews 2:14–15}}). Jesus has full authority to offer hope in a hostile world. 

- *Hades*: See study note on Revelation 6:7–8.

*Write*: In the vision, God instructs John on what to do for him (see {{Isaiah 6:9-10|Isaiah 6:9–10}}). This vision aims to help the church understand the present and future from God's viewpoint ({{Revelation 1:20|Revelation 1:20}}).

- John must record what he sees because Revelation is an important message for the churches. 

- The *angels* (or *messengers;* Greek *angelos*) of the seven churches could be: 

- the guardian angels of these churches (compare {{Matthew 18:10|Matthew 18:10}}; {{Acts 12:15|Acts 12:15}});

- the leading officials of the churches (compare {{Matthew 11:10|Matthew 11:10}}, where “messenger” is *angelos*); or

- a personification of the *ethos* (spirit or character) of the church.

The best understanding is probably a combination of 1 and 3.

- *To the angel … write*: This repeated command introducing each of the seven letters shows the message's importance. 

- Ephesus became the main city of the Roman province of Asia. It had the temple of Artemis (see {{Acts 19:23-35|Acts 19:23–35}}) and became the richest banking center in that region. The people of Ephesus were very independent. They refused help from Alexander to rebuild their temple after its destruction in the 300s BC. They argued that one god should not build a temple for another god (see Strabo, *Geography* 14.1.22). The pride of the Ephesians also led to the uproar against Paul ({{Acts 19:23-41|Acts 19:23–41}}).

The letter to the church in Ephesus speaks to Christians who follow traditions. They are faithful but have lost their early, strong love for Christ and each other (see {{Revelation 2:5|Revelation 2:5}}).

John wrote down Jesus’ messages as letters to the churches.

In the letter to the church in Ephesus Jesus recognised that the believers were suffering. They were staying faithful to Jesus. Yet he wanted them to love him and one another more deeply. Their love should be as strong as it was when they first believed in Jesus.

Jesus comforted the church in Smyrna. They were going to face hard times in the future. Some of those believers would be put to death for following Jesus. But Jesus promised to give them life that the second death couldn’t destroy.

Some in the church of Pergamum weren’t staying faithful to Jesus. They were following teachings about Jesus that weren’t true. Some of these teachings were like what the prophet Balaam taught long ago. Other teachings were from the Nicolaitans. It isn’t known exactly who the Nicolaitans were. But their teachings went against Jesus’ teachings and way of living. Jesus urged the believers in Pergamum to turn away from sin.

The seven messages to the seven churches show the condition of Christ's church when Revelation was written, and it is similar today. God still calls Christians to be faithful and honest. Those who listen to Christ's message will receive God's promised rewards. Those who do not will face judgment.

- *I know*: This repeated refrain ({{Revelation 2:9|Revelation 2:9}}, {{Revelation 2:13|13}}, {{Revelation 2:19|19}}; {{Revelation 3:1|3:1}}, {{Revelation 3:8|8}}, {{Revelation 3:15|15}}) shows Christ knows everything about his people, their actions, and their situations. 

- The Ephesian Christians had a correct understanding of their beliefs, marked by perseverance and faithfulness. They examined various claims, disciplined evil people, could tell what is true and false, and patiently suffered for their faith in Christ.

*You have abandoned your first love*: When the church began, their love for Christ and each other was strong. Struggles with false teachers and persecution caused that original love to grow cold. Correct beliefs, action, and even suffering ({{Revelation 2:2-3|Revelation 2:2–3}}) are only an empty form of Christian life if living and active love is missing ({{1 Corinthians 13:1-13|1 Corinthians 13}}).

Christ calls those who keep the faith to return to him and repent of being cold-hearted. The warning, I will come and remove your lampstand, means they would lose their status as a church. God would treat them like he did the people who abandoned their faith within Israel (see {{Romans 11:1-36|Romans 11}}).

Little is known about the Nicolaitans. Their teachings ({{Revelation 2:15|Revelation 2:15}}) suggest they ate food offered to idols and engaged in sexual immorality. The council in Jerusalem prohibited this behavior (see {{Acts 15:20|Acts 15:20}}, {{Acts 15:29|29}}). The early church father Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, said that the Nicolaitans followed the teaching of Nicolas ({{Acts 6:3-5|Acts 6:3–5}}). He believed John's writings opposed the Nicolaitan false teachings linked to Cerinthus (see 1 John Book Introduction, “Setting”).
Obeying leads to the reward of eternal life, symbolized by fruit from the tree of life ({{Revelation 22:2|Revelation 22:2}}; {{Genesis 3:22|Genesis 3:22}}).

The seaport village of Smyrna was destroyed and rebuilt many times. Like Christ, the city was once dead but is now alive. It is the only one of the seven cities that still exists today as Izmir in modern Turkey.

The letter to the church in Smyrna describes suffering Christians under intense pressures who need a message of assurance. Smyrna represents a small church that stays faithful to God despite difficult times.

- Jesus linked material poverty with the blessing of being rich in God's Kingdom ({{Matthew 5:3|Matthew 5:3}}, {{Matthew 5:10-12|10–12}}; {{Luke 6:20|Luke 6:20}}). 

- Jews without faith are criticized for siding with Satan against Christianity ({{Revelation 3:9|Revelation 3:9}}; see {{John 8:44|John 8:44}}; {{Acts 14:2-5|Acts 14:2–5}}; {{Acts 17:13|17:13}}; {{Acts 18:6|18:6}}; {{Acts 20:3|20:3}}; {{Galatians 5:11|Galatians 5:11}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:14-16|1 Thessalonians 2:14–16}}). At the Jewish council of Jamnia, Jewish leaders decided that Christians were unholy and should be excluded. John was not speaking against Jewish people as a whole. He was a Jew describing the actions of some of his fellow Jews toward both Jewish and non-Jewish Christians.

- John saw the devil as the source of human hostility against Christians.

- The period of their suffering would last ten days, symbolizing a limited time of persecution (see {{1 Peter 1:6|1 Peter 1:6}}). If they remained faithful, their reward would be the crown of eternal life. 

- even unto death: John’s student Polycarp became a martyr in Smyrna in the mid-100s AD.

Staying faithful until death is seen as a victory. Overcoming the second death means gaining eternal life (see {{Revelation 20:5-6|Revelation 20:5–6}}, {{Revelation 20:14|14}}; {{Revelation 21:8|21:8}}).

Christ's *sharp, double-edged sword* shows that these Christians would face the Lord’s harshest judgment (see {{Revelation 2:16|Revelation 2:16}}; see study note on Revelation 1:16). The *double-edged sword* was a Roman symbol of authority, representing Pergamum as the province's capital. If the church failed, Christ, the true governor of the city, would use his authority against them.

The letter to the church in Pergamum describes Christians facing temptations to compromise their morals and loyalty to God. Pergamum was the first capital of the Roman province of Asia. The city had a famous library, and its people developed the use of animal skins for writing.

- The throne of Satan might refer to the altar of Zeus on the mountain above the city or to emperor worship at the temple of Augustus. For many years, the Roman governor had his throne there, and the great temple of Athena and other shrines were also in Pergamum. Calling it Satan’s city might also refer to the temple of Asclepius, whose symbol was coiled snakes. The city was dedicated to the Roman gods and emperor worship. 

- Antipas is otherwise unknown.

- Some people in Pergamum mixed Christianity with pagan beliefs and took part in immoral activities. John compares them to Balaam, who led Israel into sin (see {{Numbers 25:1-3|Numbers 25:1–3}}; {{2 Peter 2:15|2 Peter 2:15}}; {{Jude 11|Jude 1:11}}). 

- *Nicolaitans*: see study note on Revelation 2:6.

- Those who stay faithful to Christ will receive manna, which is nourishment from heaven (see {{Exodus 16:11-36|Exodus 16:11–36}}). 

- *hidden manna*: During the exodus, people placed a jar of manna in the ark of the covenant ({{Exodus 16:33-36|Exodus 16:33–36}}). Jewish tradition said that when the Messiah (God's chosen one) comes, the ark will reappear, and people will eat manna at the messianic banquet. Jesus is the bread from heaven and the bread of life ({{John 6:32-35|John 6:32–35}}; compare {{Exodus 16:4-21|Exodus 16:4–21}}).

- A white stone was often given to winners in athletic competitions, and people commonly used a white stone for admission to special banquets or festivities. It suggests acceptance and victory. 

- The new name probably refers to the recipient’s transformed nature in Christ (see {{Genesis 17:5|Genesis 17:5}}; {{Genesis 32:28|32:28}}; {{John 1:42|John 1:42}}).

- Thyatira was an outpost city known for its many trade guilds, including weavers and dyers ({{Acts 16:14|Acts 16:14}}). 

- The flaming eyes of the Son of God show deep perception. The solid feet represent Christ's stability, contrasting with the famous Colossus of Rhodes. This enormous statue was once thought to be stable until an earthquake destroyed it in 226 BC.
The letter to the church in Thyatira warns Christians against combining their faith with pagan practices and worldly behaviors.

Jesus’ letter to the church in Thyatira shows how well he knows his followers. He knows how hard they work and how deeply they love him.

He also knows all the ways they aren’t faithful to him. Some believers in Thyatira were committing sexual sins and sins with food. This showed that they weren’t obeying Jesus as Lord. Instead they were following a false prophet that Jesus called Jezebel.

Many believers in the church in Sardis had dead faith. James had talked about dead faith in James 2:14–26. Jesus wanted them to wake up and obey God.

Other believers in Sardis were faithfully obeying Jesus. Jesus talked about this like being dressed in white clothing.
Christ praises the Thyatirans for their knowledge and understanding of everything.

The mention of Jezebel, who led Israel into idol worship and immoral behavior ({{1 Kings 16:31-33|1 Kings 16:31–33}}; {{1 Kings 21:5-26|21:5–26}}), highlights a serious issue. Like the Old Testament queen who led the worship of Baal (see {{1 Kings 16:31|1 Kings 16:31}}; {{1 Kings 18:4|18:4}}; {{1 Kings 19:1-3|19:1–3}}), this unknown Jezebel claimed to be a prophet but was leading God's people into immorality. This included sexual misconduct and forming idolatrous alliances and actions ({{Exodus 34:15-16|Exodus 34:15–16}}; {{Psalm 106:39|Psalm 106:39}}; {{Isaiah 57:7-8|Isaiah 57:7–8}}).

Through messengers like John, Christ gave this false prophet a chance to repent for her wrong teachings and actions. However, like many others, she refused (compare {{Revelation 9:20-21|Revelation 9:20–21}}).

- Christ’s judgment on this “Jezebel” and on those who follow her takes place in three stages: 

- Jezebel will suffer on a sickbed;

- her followers will experience great suffering; and

- her children will die (compare {{Acts 5:5|Acts 5:5}}, {{Acts 5:10|10}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:30|1 Corinthians 11:30}}).

This judgment is similar to the plagues on Egypt, which ended with the deaths of Egypt's firstborn sons (see {{Exodus 12:29-30|Exodus 12:29–30}}). 

- God knows people's thoughts and intentions (see {{Jeremiah 17:10|Jeremiah 17:10}}; {{Acts 1:24|Acts 1:24}}; {{Hebrews 4:12-13|Hebrews 4:12–13}}). He gives each person the judgment that person deserves (see {{Revelation 22:12|Revelation 22:12}}; {{Jeremiah 17:10|Jeremiah 17:10}}; {{Matthew 16:27|Matthew 16:27}}).

The phrase *deep things of Satan* might refer to the Gnostic god *Bythos* (which means "Depth"). In some Gnostic writings, *Bythos* is the source of other spiritual beings. His partner *Sigē (*which means "Silence") completes this divine pair. Gnostic groups often taught that people could reach salvation through secret knowledge.

- Christ promises that those who obey will share authority with him. This is symbolized by the iron rod that will break the opposition like clay pots (quoting {{Psalm 2:8-9|Psalm 2:8–9}}; compare {{Revelation 12:5|Revelation 12:5}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}). 

- The morning star is the planet Venus, which signals the coming of a new day. Here, it refers to the promise of resurrection when Christ returns ({{Revelation 22:16|Revelation 22:16}}; {{2 Peter 1:19|2 Peter 1:19}}).

- Sardis was about 80 kilometers (50 miles) east of Smyrna on the southeast highway from Pergamum and Thyatira. It was home to a large community of wealthy Jews. They were called “Sephardic” because this name came from an ancient name for the city. The city also had a strong, fortified acropolis, which often gave its people too much confidence in their own safety.

- Other churches may have thought the Christians in Sardis were active and strong. However, their focus on worldly life showed that they lacked true spiritual life.
The letter to the church in Sardis warns Christians who seem spiritually alive but are actually dead. Without true change, they will face God's judgment.

- The church in Sardis needed to wake up and pay attention. If they did not, they would face sudden judgment. The city of Sardis had experienced this kind of surprise attack twice. The first happened when the forces of Cyrus entered the city through a secret tunnel around 549 or 546 BC. The second happened in 189 BC when Antiochus III attacked the city in the same way. 

In both cases, the watchmen were not alert, and the city fell. The same would happen to the Christians there if they did not meet God's requirements (see {{Revelation 20:12|Revelation 20:12}}; {{Ephesians 2:10|Ephesians 2:10}}; {{James 2:20|James 2:20}}). 

- *like a thief*: Like the invaders in the city’s history, Christ would come suddenly (see {{Revelation 16:15|Revelation 16:15}}; {{Matthew 24:43|Matthew 24:43}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:2|1 Thessalonians 5:2}}; {{2 Peter 3:10|2 Peter 3:10}}).

- *Soiled … garments *symbolize an impure life ({{Zechariah 3:4|Zechariah 3:4}}), while *white* clothes represent purity (see {{Revelation 6:11|Revelation 6:11}}; {{Revelation 7:13-14|7:13–14}}; {{Revelation 22:14|22:14}}). 

- How they *walk* means how a person lives (see {{Genesis 17:1|Genesis 17:1}}; {{Psalm 81:13|Psalms 81:13}}; {{Psalm 82:5|82:5}}; {{Romans 8:4|Romans 8:4}}; {{Galatians 5:16|Galatians 5:16}}).

Having one's name in the *Book of Life* (see {{Revelation 20:12-15|Revelation 20:12–15}}; {{Daniel 7:10|Daniel 7:10}}) means assurance of God's acceptance and eternal life (see {{Revelation 17:8|Revelation 17:8}}; {{Revelation 20:12|20:12}}; {{Philippians 4:3|Philippians 4:3}}; see also {{Luke 10:20|Luke 10:20}}). If God erases a name, it implies condemnation and eternal death (see {{Exodus 32:32-33|Exodus 32:32–33}}; {{Psalm 69:28|Psalm 69:28}}).

- Philadelphia was located in the foothills of the Timolus Mountains, with fertile plains to the east. The city often suffered from severe earthquakes, which left it weak and poor. 

- This verse uses phrases from {{Isaiah 22:22|Isaiah 22:22}}. 

- *key of David*: Jesus the Messiah, God's chosen one, is the successor to David’s royal line. As the gatekeeper of heaven, Jesus has the authority to open and close the way to heaven (compare {{Matthew 16:19|Matthew 16:19}}).

The letter to the church in Philadelphia encourages Christians who feel weak and powerless to understand that their true strength is in Christ. This comforting message includes no words of disapproval. The kingdom of God relies not on human strength or wisdom but on God's power and authority.

The church in Philadelphia had an opportunity to share the good news with others. This is what Jesus meant about the door he had opened for them.

In 1 Corinthians 16:9 and 2 Corinthians 2:12, Paul had also written about doors like that being opened. The believers in Philadelphia didn’t have enough strength on their own. Jesus would give them the strength to do what he wanted them to do. He would make them as strong as pillars in God’s temple.

Jews who didn’t follow Jesus opposed them. Jesus promised that even those Jews would one day recognise that Jesus loves his followers.

The believers in Laodicea had become proud. They no longer recognised how much they needed Jesus. Jesus corrected them because he loved them. He was like the master returning home in the story he told in Luke 12:35–38. He wanted the believers in Laodicea to be ready to receive him when he returned. He promised to share a meal with those who received him. This showed how deeply Jesus loved them and wanted them to be joined to him.

- *I know*: See study note on Revelation 2:2–3. 

- *little strength*: Like the city of Philadelphia itself (see study note on Revelation 3:7), the Christians there were not wealthy and lacked status and power. However, Christ opened a door for them (see {{Revelation 3:7|Revelation 3:7}}) to claim his status and authority. Despite their weakness, the Philadelphia church obeyed Christ’s word and did not deny him under pressure.

- *those who belong to the synagogue of Satan*: The Christians in Philadelphia experienced mistreatment from Jews who opposed Christianity (see study note on Revelation 2:9).

- *bow down at your feet*: In ancient times, captives often had to bow before their conquerors (see {{Isaiah 49:23|Isaiah 49:23}}; {{Isaiah 60:14|60:14}}). The church’s human enemies will eventually recognize that God loves Christians.

- Jesus will protect Christians who persevere and remain faithful during difficult times (compare {{Isaiah 43:2-4|Isaiah 43:2–4}}; {{John 10:27-28|John 10:27–28}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:13|1 Corinthians 10:13}}; {{Hebrews 6:18-19|Hebrews 6:18–19}}). 

- The* hour of testing* refers to the end times when the world experiences severe difficulties.
Christians must remain faithful. They need to persevere through difficulties to keep their crown, which is their expected reward.

- Victorious Christians are secure in God's household, like pillars, and they will never have to leave it. 

- The name of God inscribed on them shows God's ownership and the security Christians enjoy (see {{Revelation 7:4|Revelation 7:4}}; {{Revelation 14:1|14:1}}). 

- The new Jerusalem is not built by humans. Instead, it is God's gift from heaven ({{Revelation 21:2-10|Revelation 21:2–10}}). 

- A new name was a sign of God's blessing (see also {{Revelation 2:17|Revelation 2:17}}). Abram, Jacob, Simon, and others received new names ({{Genesis 17:5|Genesis 17:5}}; {{Genesis 32:28|32:28}}; {{John 1:42|John 1:42}}).

- Laodicea was located 65 kilometers (40 miles) southeast of Philadelphia. It was the economic and judicial center of a region that included Colossae and Hierapolis. The people of Laodicea were proud of their independence. After a severe earthquake in AD 60, Laodicea refused help from Rome and rebuilt their city on their own, making it very beautiful (Tacitus, *Annals* 14.27). 

- *Amen*: Used as an oath, "Amen" is a promise of truth ({{Isaiah 65:16|Isaiah 65:16}}). Jesus represents the truth ({{John 8:32|John 8:32}}; {{John 14:6|14:6}}), and his message is confirmed by the truthfulness and reliability of his word. 

- The description of Christ as the faithful and true witness shows that he knew them as they truly were. Although they were wealthy and proud of their status and achievements, they did not meet God’s expectations.

The letter to the church in Laodicea warns Christians who are *lukewarm*, meaning they are not fully committed to Christ. Their inconsistent lives show loyalty only to themselves. Their behavior is so displeasing to Christ that he is ready to reject them, as if spitting them out of his mouth.

*neither cold nor hot*: The hot springs in Hierapolis were famous for their healing qualities. Colossae was equally famous for its cold, refreshing springs. In contrast, the water in Laodicea was smelly and lukewarm. Such water is unpleasant. Jesus was saying that the church's indecisive commitment to him was revolting.
Christians in Laodicea believed they were prosperous and self-sufficient (see study note on Revelation 3:14). However, Jesus saw their true spiritual state as wretched, miserable, and poor.

- Jesus advised the people of Laodicea to change their attitude from self-reliance to relying on God. 

- *buy from Me gold*: They could buy anything they wanted, but they needed heavenly treasures for spiritual riches through faith in Christ. 

- *refined by fire*: Material wealth will not survive God's cleansing by fire (compare {{1 Corinthians 3:12-15|1 Corinthians 3:12–15}}), but spiritual wealth lasts forever. 

- White garments are a symbol of spiritual purity. Laodicea was famous for its black wool cloth, a source of their wealth, which likely represents their proud and unredeemed spiritual state. 

- Laodicea's wealth also came from its famous Phrygian eye ointment, possibly used in a local eye clinic linked to the renowned physician Demosthenes Philalethes. The Laodiceans needed to obtain ointment from Christ through faith. Only his eye salve would help them see their sins and repent.

Christ will correct and guide those he loves instead of rejecting them ({{Proverbs 3:11-12|Proverbs 3:11–12}}; {{Hebrews 12:5-6|Hebrews 12:5–6}}). He remains faithful even to those who are unfaithful ({{2 Timothy 2:13|2 Timothy 2:13}}).

- A person or a church must listen for Jesus knocking and open the door to him. Christ offers a way for a church to revive when it has become spiritually weak and lost connection with him. Simply opening the door can renew their previous bond. 

- *dine with him, and he with Me*: A shared meal represents acceptance, deep friendship, and a covenant relationship ({{Revelation 19:9|Revelation 19:9}}; see {{Genesis 18:1-5|Genesis 18:1–5}}, {{Genesis 18:16-19|16–19}}; {{Exodus 12:1-31|Exodus 12:1–31}}; {{Exodus 18:12|18:12}}; {{Matthew 26:26-30|Matthew 26:26–30}}).

The reward for faith that is victorious and obedient is to sit with Christ on his throne. This picture shows great honor and closeness to Christ. It means that believers will share in his authority when he rules over the new creation.

This reward does *not* mean that Christians become divine. Only God is divine. Instead, Christians share in Christ’s victory and in the work he gives them in his kingdom ({{Revelation 20:4|Revelation 20:4}}, {{Revelation 20:6|6}}; {{Revelation 22:5|22:5}}; {{Colossians 3:1-4|Colossians 3:1–4}}; {{2 Timothy 2:12|2 Timothy 2:12}}).

- *After this I … saw*: This introductory phrase does not show the *order of events* (see also {{Revelation 7:9|Revelation 7:9}}; {{Revelation 15:5|15:5}}; {{Revelation 18:1|18:1}}; compare {{Revelation 19:1|19:1}}). Instead, it signals a new vision that John receives. 

- *Come up here*: The Lord’s voice invites John to see what will happen from God’s point of view.

The second vision John wrote about occurred in heaven. The vision was of an area in heaven where God’s throne is. Everything that John recorded until Revelation chapter 17 happened in this vision.

What John saw first was like what other prophets had seen in visions of God’s throne. Those visions are recorded in 1 Kings 22:19, Isaiah chapter 6, Ezekiel 1:26–28 and Daniel 7:9–10. The things John saw were signs of God’s complete power and glory.

The rainbow showed God’s splendour and glory. In the Bible the rainbow is a sign of God’s mercy.

John heard and saw the 24 elders and the four living creatures worshipping God. Together they are a picture of God being praised for ever by all of creation.

The description of God’s throne room is beyond what people can easily imagine. It continues the visions in {{Isaiah 6:1-4|Isaiah 6:1–4}}, {{Ezekiel 1:4-28|Ezekiel 1:4–28}}, and {{Daniel 7:9-10|Daniel 7:9–10}}, where God is seen on a powerful and majestic throne. God’s throne is a central theme in Revelation. The worship that appears throughout the rest of the book begins from this scene. God’s greatness, grace, and glory form the foundation of the church’s worship.

This section introduces upcoming visions and judgments. John presents God in his heavenly court, which is the setting for the drama of Revelation ({{Revelation 4:1-11|Revelation 4:1–11}}). The Lamb also plays a central role ({{Revelation 5:1-14|Revelation 5:1–14}}). John contrasts God's majesty with the supposed majesty of Caesar. God's power and splendor surpass any earthly ruler's ceremonial court.

By being in the Spirit, John could experience spiritual realities (see {{Revelation 1:10|Revelation 1:10}}; {{Revelation 17:3|17:3}}; {{Revelation 21:10|21:10}}; {{Ezekiel 11:1|Ezekiel 11:1}}). He could understand insights about God's presence, the heavenly realm, and God's plans in history.

Instead of creating a visual image of God ({{Exodus 20:4|Exodus 20:4}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:15-19|Deuteronomy 4:15–19}}), John uses gemstones and the rainbow ({{Genesis 9:8-17|Genesis 9:8–17}}; {{Ezekiel 1:28|Ezekiel 1:28}}) to suggest God's qualities. The rainbow represents God's grace, reminding us of God's promise to Noah ({{Genesis 9:13-17|Genesis 9:13–17}}) that he would never again flood the earth. However, in Revelation, the earth is destroyed by fire ({{Genesis 19:24-29|Genesis 19:24–29}}).

The twenty-four elders on their thrones likely represent all of God's people. They may correspond to the twelve tribes of the old covenant and the twelve apostles of the new (see {{Revelation 21:12-14|Revelation 21:12–14}}). Some people associate them with the twenty-four divisions of the Israelite priesthood ({{1 Chronicles 24:1-19|1 Chronicles 24:1–19}}). 

In this vision, the elders speak and worship in an *antiphonal* way, which means that two groups take turns speaking or singing.

- The thunder that follows flashes of lightning is a call from God to pay attention (see {{Revelation 8:5|Revelation 8:5}}; {{Revelation 11:19|11:19}}; {{Revelation 16:18|16:18}}). 

- *Before the throne burned seven torches of fire*: In ancient times, people placed torches before rulers to show their authority. These torches with burning flames represent the perfect spirit of God.

- *a sea of glass, as clear as crystal*: The most noticeable part of ancient theaters was the bright mosaic floor where the orchestra performed. This design helped people see the scene clearly (compare {{Revelation 15:2-4|Revelation 15:2–4}}). 

- The four living beings represent all of creation. 

- *covered with eyes*: This phrase likely means they had knowledge or understanding. In the ancient world, figures were often covered with a feature to highlight a quality (for example, statues of Artemis were covered with breasts to emphasize fertility). Compare {{Ezekiel 1:18|Ezekiel 1:18}}.

These four creatures symbolize different types of beings: 

- a lion represents wild animals,

- an ox represents domesticated animals,

- a human represents humanity, and

- an eagle represents birds (see {{Ezekiel 1:10|Ezekiel 1:10}}).

These figures come from {{Ezekiel 1:1-28|Ezekiel 1}} (cherubim) and {{Isaiah 6:1-13|Isaiah 6}} (seraphim). They likely represent the best of creation as worshiping God. Missing from this group of created beings are fish. Ancient people often connected fish with the dangerous or evil sea (see {{Revelation 21:1|Revelation 21:1}}). Insects are also missing. In Revelation, insects are linked to locusts that belong to the evil kingdom (see {{Revelation 9:1-11|Revelation 9:1–11}}).

- *Day and night*: The four beings continuously praised God's main qualities: 

- his holiness, 

- his power (the Almighty), and 

- his eternity (see study note on Revelation 1:4). 

- *Holy, holy, holy* comes from {{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 6:3}} and is the highest form of worship in Scripture. Repeating something two times shows strong emphasis. Repeating it three times shows the highest level of emphasis.

- The twenty-four elders, who speak in an antiphonal chorus (two groups taking turns), give a divine perspective on creation.

- *One seated on the throne*: This shows a common Jewish practice of not speaking God’s name directly.

- *Worthy are You*: This phrase is never used for God in the Old Testament. However, people in Rome often used it when they worshiped the emperor. In Revelation, it is clear that only God deserves worship.

- *You created all things*: Many people in the ancient world believed their gods were too busy to care about humans. But God is Almighty in a real and active way. He created all things and continues to rule as Creator and Lord. In Revelation, creation shows that God is in complete control of the world (see {{Revelation 3:14|Revelation 3:14}}; {{Revelation 10:6|10:6}}; {{Revelation 14:7|14:7}}; {{Revelation 21:1|21:1}}). 

- *by Your will they exist and were created*: God had a purpose for everything he made.

- The scroll, like a dramatic script, describes God's plan for the world ({{Psalm 139:16|Psalm 139:16}}). 

- The right hand represents God's gracious authority and power (see {{Revelation 1:17|Revelation 1:17}}, {{Revelation 1:20|20}}). 

- The writing on both sides of the scroll shows that God's plans for history are full and complete. 

- *sealed with seven seals*: God has placed his purposes for history in something that cannot be opened by human effort ({{Isaiah 29:11-12|Isaiah 29:11–12}}; {{Daniel 8:26|Daniel 8:26}}). His purposes will be fulfilled only when the seals are broken (see {{Revelation 5:4|Revelation 5:4}}).

What was written on the scroll were God’s words about what was going to happen. They were about his plan for heaven and earth. The one who opened the scroll would put God’s plan into effect. No one could do this but Jesus.

Jesus was described as the Root of David. This was a way to talk about Jesus being the Messiah from David’s family line. He was described as the Lion of Judah. This was a way to talk about Jesus being from Judah’s family line. It meant that he was the king God had promised to send. It also described Jesus’ strength and power.

Jesus is also the Lamb of God. This name described how Jesus wins his victory through being weak and humble. He wins through the power of love that sacrifices everything for others. The Lamb looked as if he had been put to death. This is because Jesus had died on the cross but had been raised from the dead.

The elders and the living creatures praised him for being worthy to open the scroll. Jesus was worthy because of what he had done. He had rescued people from the power of sin, death and evil. He had made them God’s people. People from every tribe, people group and nation believe in him. He makes them one in God’s royal family. Because he does this, the Lamb is worthy of honour.

The angels sang about this. All of creation worshipped the Lamb and God. In Philippians 2:10 the apostle Paul wrote about this happening.
John introduces the Lamb, Jesus Christ, who is the main figure in Revelation and God's chosen one to fulfill his plans.
At first, no one in the entire universe seemed to have the divine authority or power to answer the angel’s call.

John cried because he feared he would not learn about God's plan for history, even though it was promised to him ({{Revelation 4:1|Revelation 4:1}}; see {{Revelation 10:4|10:4}}). His tears show how important the revelation was to him.

- Titles for Jesus such as *the Lion … of Judah* (see {{Genesis 49:9-10|Genesis 49:9–10}}) and* the Root of David* (see {{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}), are Old Testament metaphors for the Messiah (see {{Jeremiah 23:5|Jeremiah 23:5}}; {{Jeremiah 30:9|30:9}}; {{John 7:42|John 7:42}}). 

- Because Jesus won the victory at the cross ({{John 16:33|John 16:33}}), he is the only one worthy to open the scroll and reveal God’s purposes ({{Revelation 4:11|Revelation 4:11}}; {{Revelation 5:2|5:2}}, {{Revelation 5:12|12}}). God’s plan for history centers around Jesus and his actions. His connection to the scroll shows his control of history.

- The Jews expected the Messiah, God's chosen one, to appear as a powerful lion. Instead, Jesus came as a lamb ({{John 1:29|John 1:29}}, {{John 1:36|36}}; {{Acts 8:32-35|Acts 8:32–35}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7}}; {{1 Peter 1:19|1 Peter 1:19}}). The lamb, once slaughtered but now standing, symbolizes the death and resurrection of Jesus. 

- The Lamb’s seven horns are a symbol of his complete power, and the seven eyes are a symbol of his complete knowledge (see {{Zechariah 4:10|Zechariah 4:10}}). He is also fully connected to the perfect spirit of God ({{Revelation 1:4|Revelation 1:4}}).

- *fell down before the Lamb*: The crucified and risen Christ has the divine authority to start the events of this age. He is fully worthy of worship. 

- The prayers of God's people play a significant role in the judgments and plagues ({{Revelation 6:9-11|Revelation 6:9–11}}; {{Revelation 8:2-5|8:2–5}}).

- The entire created order sings a new song of praise to the lamb (compare {{Revelation 14:1-5|Revelation 14:1–5}}; {{Psalm 149:1|Psalm 149:1}}; {{Isaiah 42:10|Isaiah 42:10}}). 

- The lamb is worthy because his sacrifice earned him the right to open the scroll's seals and carry out God's plans in history. 

- The song highlights the meaning of the good news about Jesus ({{1 Peter 1:18-25|1 Peter 1:18–25}}).

Describing God's people as a kingdom of priests who will achieve ultimate victory and reign with Christ reflects Jesus as both king ({{Romans 1:3|Romans 1:3}}) and high priest ({{Hebrews 6:20|Hebrews 6:20}}).
A massive angelic choir, with thousands and millions of voices, responds in turn. All of heaven answers creation's acknowledgment of Christ's sacrifice.
This doxology (a short statement of praise) gives Jesus divine honors, which are usually only for God (see {{Revelation 4:11|Revelation 4:11}}; {{Revelation 5:13|5:13}}; {{Revelation 7:12|7:12}}).

The second antiphonal response echoes from every creature, including those under the earth (the place of the dead) and in the sea (often linked with evil). This may suggest that even those rebelling against God must respond ({{Isaiah 45:23-25|Isaiah 45:23–25}}; {{Romans 14:11|Romans 14:11}}; {{Philippians 2:10-11|Philippians 2:10–11}}).

The dramatic introduction of the lamb ({{Revelation 5:1-14|Revelation 5:1–14}}) ends with the living beings ({{Revelation 4:6-9|4:6–9}}). Their *Amen* affirms the truth of John's vision, while the twenty-four elders bow in worship.

Seven seals kept the scroll shut. They had to be opened to show God’s plan for heaven and earth.

This was the first set of seven things that prepared the world for God’s plan. What John saw in the vision in heaven led to things that happened on earth.

When the Lamb opened the first four seals, John saw horses with their riders. These were signs of evil things that happen and that human beings do to one another.

Humans seek to have victory over one another like the rider on the white horse. Like the rider on the red horse, they destroy peace. Like the rider on the black horse, they deal with money unfairly. Like the rider on the pale horse, they destroy and murder one another.

The Lamb didn’t send these troubles to the earth. The opened seals revealed or uncovered how evil things already were on earth. Yet the Lamb and the four living creatures made something clear. God has authority over the world no matter how evil it is.

The four horses and their riders (see {{Zechariah 1:8-11|Zechariah 1:8–11}}; {{Zechariah 6:1-8|6:1–8}}) represent the world's power structures. Their actions lead mainly to war, violence, economic imbalance, and death. Because of this, it is useless to place our hope in these human systems of power.
The Lamb breaks the seven seals to reveal the significance of history from God’s point of view.

Three sets of seven judgments (the seals, trumpets, and bowls) are central to Revelation. Some believe these judgments happen in a sequence, one after another, totaling twenty-one judgments. 

However, it is more likely that the relationship is cyclical, similar to other Jewish apocalyptic writings (compare {{Daniel 2:1-49|Daniel 2}}, {{Daniel 7:1-28|7}}, {{Daniel 8:1-27|8}}, {{Daniel 11:1-45|11}}). Each set of judgments becomes more intense and adds new details about God's judgment on those who rebel against him. In this view, all three cycles end at the same time, with the return of Christ.

- Some people think the rider on a white horse is Christ, like in {{Revelation 19:11|Revelation 19:11}}. But the only similarity between these two images is the horse. The four riders represent a destructive and senseless world. It has no redeeming qualities. 

- A bow is a weapon made of a curved piece of wood and a string. People shoot arrows with it. The bow was a common Greco-Roman military equipment. Here it is as a symbol of war. 

- *to overcome and conquer*: The repeated use of the Greek word *nikaō* (which means "conquer") shows this rider is powerful. The focus on war and conquest shows the deep sinfulness of humanity.

The red horse symbolizes bloody violence on earth. The Roman Empire promised peace (the *pax Romana*), but widespread violence was the grim reality. This rider represents slaughter, including civil unrest and ethnic cleansing.

The black horse represents economic and social trouble. The rider carries scales, which were used in ancient commerce, to show this problem. The vision shows extreme inflation. A worker would have to spend a full day’s wages to buy one loaf of wheat bread or three loaves of barley. But the prices of luxury items, such as oil and wine, would stay the same. This is a picture of severe social and economic imbalance.

- When the fourth seal is opened, a terrifying horse appears. In the ancient world, a pale green color was used to show the color of a dead body.

- *Hades*: In Greek thought, Hades was the underworld for spirits without bodies. The Hebrew concept of *Sheol,* the place of the dead ({{1 Samuel 28:15|1 Samuel 28:15}}), was similar. 

- The death of one-fourth of the people on earth shows that the final judgment has not yet come (contrast {{Revelation 6:16-17|Revelation 6:16–17}}). 

- This set of four woes (sword, famine, disease, and wild animals; compare {{Ezekiel 14:21|Ezekiel 14:21}}) summarizes the hardships of life on earth. The world cannot provide hope for humanity.
Instead of following the destructive ways of the world, the martyrs (those who died for their faith) chose to give their lives because they remained faithful to the word of God.
In contrast to the world's destructive ways ({{Revelation 6:1-8|Revelation 6:1–8}}), the fifth seal introduces Christian martyrs who ask how God intends to deal with evil.

When the fifth seal was opened, John saw souls who were begging God for justice. The soul is the spiritual part of a human being. These were people who had been killed for following Jesus. They waited under the golden altar. They were waiting for God to bring judgement against the people who had killed them.

When the sixth seal was opened, things happened on earth that scared people. The things that John described were common signs in apocalyptic writings. They were signs of important events that brought about big changes in people’s lives. Everyone on earth was afraid and trying to hide. They realised that God’s anger isn’t like the anger of human beings. The Lamb’s anger is against everything that opposes God. His anger doesn’t harm people who trust in him.

- The martyrs called out to God because they trusted his power to address their grievances. 

- *How long*: Is God slow to act? Will justice be served? God acts decisively (see {{Revelation 6:12-14|Revelation 6:12–14}}). His wrath ({{Revelation 6:16-17|Revelation 6:16–17}}) should be understood as justice, fairness, and righteousness (see {{Exodus 34:5-7|Exodus 34:5–7}}; {{Nehemiah 9:17|Nehemiah 9:17}}; {{Psalm 103:8|Psalms 103:8}}; {{Psalm 145:8|145:8}}; {{Joel 2:13|Joel 2:13}}; {{Jonah 4:2|Jonah 4:2}}; {{Romans 2:6-11|Romans 2:6–11}}). 

- *avenge our blood*: This plea for God’s justice follows the pattern of psalms calling for vengeance (see {{Psalm 6:3|Psalms 6:3}}; {{Psalm 74:10|74:10}}; {{Psalm 79:5|79:5}}; {{Psalm 80:4|80:4}}; {{Psalm 137:1-9|137:1–9}}). It also reflects the covenant curses of {{Deuteronomy 28:53-57|Deuteronomy 28:53–57}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:35|32:35}} (quoted in {{Romans 12:19|Romans 12:19}}).

- A white robe symbolizes the victory of the martyrs and God's complete acceptance. 

- *told to rest*: Death is a state of rest (compare {{John 11:11-12|John 11:11–12}}) where martyrs await God's justice. 

- *the full number*: Only God knows how many Christians will be killed because of their faith before the end. In his complete authority and power, God will achieve his purposes through his martyred children and will vindicate them at the right time. 

- *brothers*: The Greek word *adelphoi* refers to both male and female members of the same family.

These violent and world-shaking signs are linked in Scripture to the day of the Lord. On this day, God’s judgment will disrupt the entire created order (see {{Isaiah 13:4-12|Isaiah 13:4–12}}; {{Isaiah 34:1-4|34:1–4}}; {{Joel 2:1-32|Joel 2:1–32}}; {{Zephaniah 2:1-3|Zephaniah 2:1–3}}; {{Mark 13:1-37|Mark 13:1–37}}).
The opening of the sixth seal provides a preview of the end of the world.

- *every slave and free man hid*: When God’s judgment comes, people who are not redeemed will be terrified. They will try to hide in a safe place, but they will not succeed ({{Isaiah 2:19-21|Isaiah 2:19–21}}; {{Ezekiel 38:20|Ezekiel 38:20}}; {{Hosea 10:8|Hosea 10:8}}; {{Luke 23:30|Luke 23:30}}). The prophets often warned that this great day would bring wrath and judgment ({{Isaiah 13:6-11|Isaiah 13:6–11}}; {{Joel 1:15|Joel 1:15}}; {{Amos 5:18|Amos 5:18}}; {{Zephaniah 1:14-15|Zephaniah 1:14–15}}).

- The key question about God’s judgment is, who can survive? ({{Malachi 3:2|Malachi 3:2}}). God’s children will be happy to see him ({{Revelation 5:13-14|Revelation 5:13–14}}; {{Revelation 14:3-5|14:3–5}}) because they understand God’s answer to the martyrs’ call for justice ({{Revelation 6:9-11|6:9–11}}), and they have nothing to fear from God’s judgment ({{Acts 10:34-36|Acts 10:34–36}}; {{Romans 5:1-2|Romans 5:1–2}}). Those who have harmed God’s people will tremble in fear as they face the wrath of the Lamb.

- *Do not … until*: God commands the four angels to hold back the winds for a short time. They must not harm the earth, the sea, or the trees until the servants of God receive his seal on their foreheads.

- The seal of the living God signifies belonging to God's family; God owns and protects his people ({{2 Corinthians 1:22|2 Corinthians 1:22}}; {{Ephesians 1:13-14|Ephesians 1:13–14}}). In ancient times, sealing or tattooing showed ownership. 

- The angel carrying the seal identified God's people, answering who would survive God's wrath ({{Revelation 6:17|Revelation 6:17}}; see {{Ezekiel 9:3-8|Ezekiel 9:3–8}}; {{John 17:14-15|John 17:14–15}}) and furthering the promise of protection ({{Revelation 3:10|Revelation 3:10}}; see also {{Revelation 11:1-2|11:1–2}}).
The first vision in the interlude shows how God protects his faithful followers from any ultimate harm.

Before the Lamb opened the seventh seal on the scroll, John saw a different seal. It was God’s official seal. Whatever was marked with this seal belonged to God.

With his ears John heard the number of people that the angels marked with God’s seal. It was 144,000 and the people were from the 12 tribes of Israel.

Then with his eyes John saw the huge crowd of God’s people. They were from all times and places and there were too many to count. The Lamb’s blood was the seal of God that they had been marked with. This meant that these people believed the good news about Jesus’ sacrifice on the cross. Having this mark meant that God would bring them safely through suffering.

The elder was talking about the suffering that would come on judgement day. The four angels holding back the winds were a picture of that judgement. Being sealed as God’s people doesn’t mean that believers won’t suffer. It doesn’t mean that they won’t be killed for following Jesus. But it means that the Lamb will guide them as their shepherd. It means that God will comfort them and provide everything that they need. It means that they will be part of the crowd that worships God for ever.

John saw God’s people standing around the Lamb and around God’s throne. Together with the angels, the elders and the living creatures, they were praising God. This was a picture of what would happen after God had judged all things. It was a picture of heaven and earth after God had made all things new. It was a picture of the new creation. This vision would bring hope and strength to the churches John was writing to.

Three interludes occur in {{Revelation 6:1-14:20|Revelation 6–14}} ({{Revelation 7:1-17|Revelation 7}}; {{Revelation 10:1-11:14|10:1–11:14}}; {{Revelation 12:1-14:20|12:1–14:20}}). These interludes explain the place of God’s holy people and help readers understand the scenes that came before them. In this first interlude, which appears before the seventh seal is opened, two visions show how God protects his people and confirms his calling on them.

Who are the 144,000? This list of the tribes of Israel does not match the twelve physical tribes exactly. Instead, it shows that God knows exactly who belongs to him. By the 90s AD, Israel’s twelve tribes no longer existed. Ten tribes were scattered when Assyria conquered the northern kingdom of Israel ({{2 Kings 17:1-41|2 Kings 17:1–41}}). 

The early Christian church saw itself symbolically as the Israel of God ({{Matthew 19:28|Matthew 19:28}}; {{Romans 2:28-29|Romans 2:28–29}}; {{Romans 9:6-8|9:6–8}}; {{Galatians 3:29|Galatians 3:29}}; {{Galatians 6:16|6:16}}; {{Philippians 3:3|Philippians 3:3}}). The *144,000* likely represent all faithful Christians (compare {{Revelation 14:1-5|Revelation 14:1–5}}; {{Revelation 21:12-17|21:12–17}}). 

The list starts with Judah, the royal tribe of Jesus, but replaces Dan with Manasseh, one of Joseph's two tribes. The tribe of Dan fell into idolatry ({{Judges 18:14-31|Judges 18:14–31}}; {{1 Kings 12:25-30|1 Kings 12:25–30}}), and early Christians saw it as the symbol of evil.

- This large group of believers ({{Revelation 7:14|Revelation 7:14}}) is too numerous to count, fulfilling God's promises to Abraham ({{Genesis 15:5|Genesis 15:5}}; {{Genesis 17:4-5|17:4–5}}; {{Romans 4:16-24|Romans 4:16–24}}; {{Galatians 3:29|Galatians 3:29}}). 

- White robes ({{Revelation 6:11|Revelation 6:11}}) and palm branches ({{John 12:13|John 12:13}}) are ancient symbols of victory and success. They add to the celebration that happens after God ends the hostile world.
The second vision in the interlude shows heaven filled with a crowd so large that no one can count it. They rejoice because they are safe in Christ, and all their tears and sorrows have ended.
In ancient times, victory parades celebrated conquerors with loud chants. The shout of *Salvation* means "victory" or "deliverance." It honors God's triumph and prepares readers for his rule.

The angels, elders, and four living beings all bowed before God. They responded together with a sevenfold doxology (complete praise) to honor God's eternal nature. The word *Amen* comes before and after the doxology, serving as a strong affirmation of God's victory.

- *who have come out of*: See {{Revelation 6:9|Revelation 6:9}}; {{Revelation 20:4|20:4}}. 

- *the great tribulation*: A period of terrible and distressing events (see {{Revelation 1:9|Revelation 1:9}}; {{Revelation 2:9-10|2:9–10}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:30-31|Deuteronomy 4:30–31}}; {{Matthew 24:21-22|Matthew 24:21–22}}; {{Acts 14:22|Acts 14:22}}).

- *they have washed their robes … in the blood of the Lamb*: This description is a symbol of Christ’s redeeming death for them. 

- *made them white*: This phrase shows their victory over sin and death and their acceptance by God into eternal life.

- *serve Him day and night*: Serving God is a constant duty for Christians. 

- God's temple represents his presence (also see {{Revelation 11:19|Revelation 11:19}}; compare {{Revelation 21:22|21:22}}).

- For those living in deserts, water and shade from the sun feel like paradise (see also {{Revelation 21:6|Revelation 21:6}}; {{Revelation 22:1|22:1}}, {{Revelation 22:17|17}}; {{Psalm 23:1-2|Psalm 23:1–2}}; {{Ezekiel 47:1-12|Ezekiel 47:1–12}}; {{John 7:37-38|John 7:37–38}}). 

- *in the center of the throne*: The Lamb is closely connected with God. 

- Christ’s role as the shepherd of God’s people (compare {{Psalm 23:1-6|Psalm 23}}; {{Matthew 15:24|Matthew 15:24}}; {{John 10:3|John 10:3}}, {{John 10:11|11}}, {{John 10:14|14}}; {{Hebrews 13:20|Hebrews 13:20}}; {{1 Peter 2:25|1 Peter 2:25}}) means he protects and provides for the sheep, bringing hope and salvation to his people (see {{Ezekiel 34:11-16|Ezekiel 34:11–16}}, {{Ezekiel 34:23-24|23–24}}).

- The opening of the seventh seal ends the first act and starts a dramatic silence. This silence suggests the mystery of God's actions in the world ({{Revelation 10:4|Revelation 10:4}}; {{1 Kings 19:11-12|1 Kings 19:11–12}}). This mysterious silence may be similar to God's rest on the seventh day of creation ({{Genesis 2:1-3|Genesis 2:1–3}}; see also {{Hebrews 4:1-11|Hebrews 4:1–11}}). 

- *half an hour*: This short pause comes before the second act of divine judgment, when God will answer his people's prayers.

When the seventh seal was opened, there was a time of silence in John’s vision. During this quiet, the prayers of God’s people were heard in heaven.

The prayers looked to John like an offering made with incense by an angel. The answer to the prayers looked like fire from the golden altar. The angel threw the fire to earth.

The incense and fire were a sign of how prayer is powerful and important. In James 5:16 James had written about the power of believers’ prayers. The incense and fire were also a sign of how God answers his people’s prayers. Their prayers are part of how God’s plans for the world move forward.

When the seventh seal was opened, a group of angels received seven trumpets. John’s visions were based on groups of sevens.

Angels sound trumpets dramatically to announce an approaching end (see {{Isaiah 27:13|Isaiah 27:13}}; {{Zechariah 9:14|Zechariah 9:14}}; {{Matthew 24:31|Matthew 24:31}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:52|1 Corinthians 15:52}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:16|1 Thessalonians 4:16}}).

This scene in heaven shows the preparation for the seven trumpets of judgment. It continues the theme of God receiving and answering prayers ({{Revelation 5:8|Revelation 5:8}}; {{Revelation 6:9-11|6:9–11}}).

- The second series of judgments involves seven trumpets. Like the first series ({{Revelation 6:1-8|Revelation 6:1–8:1}}), it includes a pause ({{Revelation 10:1-11:14|10:1–11:14}}; compare {{Revelation 7:1-17|7:1–17}}) and concludes with a view of God's eternal kingdom ({{Revelation 11:15-19|11:15–19}}; see {{Revelation 7:9-8:1|7:9–8:1}}). 

- The trumpet judgments are similar to the ten plagues of Egypt ({{Exodus 7:14-11:10|Exodus 7:14–11:10}}). They aim to show that earthly gods (or evil powers) are powerless and to clearly demonstrate God's power and control.

The prayers of God's people ask for God's final justice and judgment ({{Revelation 6:10-11|Revelation 6:10–11}}; see also {{Revelation 5:8|5:8}}; {{Ezra 9:5-6|Ezra 9:5–6}}; {{Psalm 141:2|Psalm 141:2}}; {{Daniel 9:21|Daniel 9:21}}). The mix of incense and prayers that reaches God's presence shows that God hears them (see {{Revelation 6:9-11|Revelation 6:9–11}}) and is ready to act.

- The angel throwing fire down to earth marks the dramatic start of God's judgment (see {{Genesis 19:24|Genesis 19:24}}; {{Exodus 9:23|Exodus 9:23}}; {{Leviticus 10:2|Leviticus 10:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:3|Deuteronomy 9:3}}; {{2 Kings 1:10|2 Kings 1:10}}). 

- *thunder, lightning … earthquake*: These disasters remind us of God's power, presence, and judgment (also {{Revelation 11:19|Revelation 11:19}}; {{Revelation 16:18|16:18}}; see {{Exodus 19:18-19|Exodus 19:18–19}}; {{1 Kings 19:11-12|1 Kings 19:11–12}}; {{Isaiah 29:6|Isaiah 29:6}}).

John recorded the first four trumpets being blown one after the other.

The things that happened when the trumpets were blown were like the plagues in Egypt.

Yet the judgement that John saw after each trumpet reached far beyond only one country.

John saw that one third of different things in the world were destroyed.

These numbers were signs. They meant that huge troubles came and much of God’s creation was destroyed.

- Hail and fire mixed with blood show the destruction of plant life, similar to the seventh plague on Egypt (see {{Exodus 9:13-35|Exodus 9:13–35}}; {{Joel 2:31|Joel 2:31}}; {{Acts 2:19|Acts 2:19}}). 

- *was burned up, along with … all the green grass*: Nothing escapes God's judgment. 

- This vision does not need to align with {{Revelation 9:4|Revelation 9:4}} because each scene is independent and conveys its own message.

Each of the first four trumpets affects one-third of its target (see {{Ezekiel 5:1-4|Ezekiel 5:1–4}}, {{Ezekiel 5:12|12}}; {{Zechariah 13:8|Zechariah 13:8}}). This does not convey an exact measurement. Instead, it shows that God's judgment on the earth is starting but has not reached its peak. Together, the first four trumpets deliver a unified message of judgment on the entire physical world (as with {{Revelation 6:1-8|Revelation 6:1–8}}).

- *the sea turned to blood*: This judgment is like the first plague on Egypt (see {{Exodus 7:14-25|Exodus 7:14–25}}; {{Psalm 78:44|Psalm 78:44}}). 

- The mountain of fire resembles the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, which destroyed ships and sea life (see Pliny the Younger, *Letters* 6.16.1–22).

The star named *Wormwood* (a shrubby plant that produces a bitter extract) is symbolic, not physical. Bitter water is linked to judgment from early in Israel’s history ({{Exodus 15:22-26|Exodus 15:22–26}}; {{Numbers 5:18|Numbers 5:18}}; {{Jeremiah 9:13-16|Jeremiah 9:13–16}}; {{Jeremiah 23:15|23:15}}). The message is that widespread judgment has started.

- *the fourth angel*: On the fourth day of creation, God made the sun, the moon, and the stars ({{Genesis 1:14-19|Genesis 1:14–19}}). 

- *the stars were darkened*: This judgment replicates the ninth plague in Egypt ({{Exodus 10:21-23|Exodus 10:21–23}}).

- In ancient times, people saw the eagle as a messenger from God (see *4 Ezra* 11:7–8; *2 Baruch* 77:19–26). 

- *Woe! Woe! Woe*: A threefold announcement would be seen as a message from God (see {{Acts 10:16|Acts 10:16}}). 

- The terror (Greek *ouai*), which sounded like an eagle's screech, was directed against those who were not among God's faithful (see {{Revelation 6:10|Revelation 6:10}}; {{Revelation 9:4|9:4}}, {{Revelation 9:20|20}}).

After the fifth trumpet was blown, a pit called the Abyss was opened.

Monsters like locusts came out of the Abyss and hurt people. The monsters obeyed an angel named the Destroyer.

John wasn’t talking about a real hole deep in the ground. He wasn’t talking about real locusts that looked like monsters. The monsters and the deep pit were signs about evil and evil spiritual beings.

They showed the terrible things that evil would do when God allowed it to. In John’s visions recorded in Revelation, God didn’t cause the harm. He allowed what was evil to do what it wanted to do.

John’s visions showed what would happen when God doesn’t hold evil back.

The fifth trumpet is the first of the three terrors ({{Revelation 8:13|Revelation 8:13}}). It brings a judgment of locusts from the bottomless pit, a place of horror. Ancient cultures thought the ocean depths, or the *Abyss*, was a home for demonic forces (see study note on Genesis 1:2).

The fifth and sixth trumpets show how God's judgment affects people worldwide and highlight how worthless it is to resist God. These judgments should lead to repentance, but they do not. Sin controls people so much that they choose to worship the evil forces that harm them instead of repenting and turning to God.
The smoke from the pit made the sky dark, similar to the plague in Egypt ({{Exodus 10:21-29|Exodus 10:21–29}}; see {{Matthew 27:45|Matthew 27:45}}).

The locusts come down to earth from the smoke. They have the power to sting like scorpions. They are fiercer than those in the Egyptian plague (see {{Exodus 10:14-15|Exodus 10:14–15}}). Instead of eating plants, these locusts attack people like stinging scorpions. Only people without the seal of God (see {{Revelation 7:1-8|Revelation 7:1–8}}) experience this painful judgment. The stings cause painful torture but do not cause death ({{Revelation 9:5-6|Revelation 9:5–6}}).

*torment them for five months*: This time period is a symbolically complete number based on the fingers on a hand. It is also the normal life span of locusts, suggesting that their entire purpose was to torture people.

- Some people view these locusts as symbols of attack helicopters, missiles, or other modern weapons. However, they originate from the Abyss, not from human creation. The description of these creatures, based on the appearance of locusts, is intended to cause fear and disgust. 

- Their gold crowns show that their torment affects much of the earth.

- The king of the locusts is identified in three ways: 

- as the angel from the bottomless pit, likely different from the fallen star in {{Revelation 9:1|Revelation 9:1}}, who unlocked the abyss instead of coming from it;

- as Abaddon (meaning "destruction"), often associated with death (see {{Job 28:22|Job 28:22}}; {{Psalm 88:11|Psalm 88:11}}); and

- as Apollyon, the Destroyer (see {{1 Corinthians 10:10|1 Corinthians 10:10}}). 

- Although John does not directly link the devil with this king of the locusts, the prince of demons is associated with Satan in the Gospels ({{Mark 3:22-26|Mark 3:22–26}}; see {{Matthew 12:24-27|Matthew 12:24–27}}; {{Luke 11:15-18|Luke 11:15–18}}). The New Testament also identifies the devil as the prince of this world ({{John 12:31|John 12:31}}; {{John 14:30|14:30}}; {{John 16:11|16:11}}) and the prince of the power of the air ({{Ephesians 2:2|Ephesians 2:2}}), suggesting he likely represents Satan. There is also a link to the Roman emperor Domitian, whose patron god Apollo was symbolized by the locust.

- The four horns of the gold altar (see {{Revelation 8:3|Revelation 8:3}}) appear with the sixth trumpet blast. Many excavations have found altars with pointed horns at their four corners (see study note on Exodus 27:2). 

- The voice has God's authority to command the release of the four angels. 

- These angels are bound, indicating their evil nature (compare {{Revelation 20:2|Revelation 20:2}}; *1 Enoch* 10; contrast {{Revelation 7:1|Revelation 7:1}}). Their location at the great Euphrates River likely refers to Assyria and Babylon, empires that destroyed the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, symbolizing destruction (see {{2 Kings 17:22-24|2 Kings 17:22–24}}; {{2 Kings 25:1-11|25:1–11}}).

After the sixth trumpet was blown, a huge army attacked people. Monsters like horses killed one third of all people. The monsters and their riders came from across the river Euphrates.

John wasn’t talking about real horses and riders attacking in that area of the world. The army of monsters and riders were pictures of things that nations fear. They fear being attacked by powerful enemies from other countries. They were also pictures of evil and evil spiritual beings. These were more signs of what happens when God doesn’t hold evil back.

Then John explained what the plagues were meant to accomplish. The plagues were warnings to get people’s attention so that they would stop sinning. People worshipped demons and statues instead of the true God. They did sinful things against other people. God wants people to turn away from their sin and to follow Jesus. But in John’s vision people didn’t repent even after the terrible plagues.
*hour and day and month and year*: This four-part time designation shows that even evil forces must follow God's timing.

- The connection between the four angels and their army is unclear. 

- *two hundred million*: This number symbolizes an extremely large group that cannot be counted. Even at its greatest strength, the ancient Roman army with twenty-one legions numbered only about 126,000 soldiers. It is not useful to use this number to identify any specific country with such an overwhelming destructive force.

- The riders wore armor in colors matching their horses' plagues: 

- red for fire, 

- blue for smoke, and 

- yellow for sulfur. 

These are signs of judgment in Scripture (see {{Revelation 14:10-11|Revelation 14:10–11}}; {{Revelation 19:20|19:20}}; {{Genesis 19:24-28|Genesis 19:24–28}}; {{Psalm 11:6|Psalm 11:6}}; {{Ezekiel 38:22|Ezekiel 38:22}}; {{Luke 17:29|Luke 17:29}}). 

- The horses resemble the terrifying monsters from Greek stories depicted on ancient buildings and celebrated in old dramas. 

- *A third*: See study note on Revelation 8:7–12.

- Even when faced with plagues and death, people do not automatically repent. They often continue their evil actions and worship demons and idols (things from the created world) instead of worshiping the Creator (see {{Revelation 13:4|Revelation 13:4}}; {{Revelation 14:9-10|14:9–10}}; {{Romans 1:25|Romans 1:25}}; {{1 Corinthians 8:4|1 Corinthians 8:4}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:19-22|10:19–22}}). 

- *murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft*: What people worship reflects how they live (see {{Revelation 21:8|Revelation 21:8}}; {{Revelation 22:15|22:15}}; {{Romans 1:23|Romans 1:23}}, {{Romans 1:29-32|29–32}}). 

- Revelation shows how strongly sin controls people who do not believe. It is not logical for people to worship powers or beings that harm, torture, or kill them. Yet sin and rebellion against God can deceive people and draw them in with great power.

*another mighty angel* (see {{Revelation 5:2|Revelation 5:2}}; {{Revelation 7:2|7:2}}; compare {{Revelation 1:12-16|1:12–16}}): This angel looks like the large bronze Colossus that stood as a symbol of human power in the harbor of Rhodes for several decades before an earthquake toppled it in the late 200s BC. The statue was still broken when John wrote Revelation. It was about 100 feet tall and represented the sun god, Helios. 

The angel was surrounded by a cloud, suggesting he was larger than the Rhodes statue and, by implication, all idols. 

The rainbow over his head reminds us that the enthroned God is encircled by a rainbow ({{Revelation 4:3|Revelation 4:3}}), a biblical symbol of God’s covenant with humanity ({{Genesis 9:8-17|Genesis 9:8–17}}).

John wasn’t supposed to share with others everything he saw in the visions God gave him. That was the case with what he heard when the seven thunders spoke.

Yet God did want John to share what was written on the little scroll. This was a message that one of God’s angels gave to John. In the vision, John ate the scroll. This was like when the prophet Ezekiel ate a scroll many years before (Ezekiel 3:1–4).

The scroll John ate tasted sweet but then hurt his stomach. This was a picture of how John needed to have God’s words inside of him. Then he could share them with others. John shared them in the rest of the book of Revelation.

The sweet part of the message was that God was going to save his people. The bitter part was that many people would refuse God’s salvation and would be destroyed.

This interlude between the sixth and seventh trumpets has two parts: 

- the seven thunders and the small scroll ({{Revelation 10:1-11|Revelation 10:1–11}}), and

- the two witnesses ({{Revelation 11:1-13|Revelation 11:1–13}}).

The interlude ends with the announcement that the second terror is over ({{Revelation 11:14|Revelation 11:14}}).

- Although the scroll is small, it is still very important. It reveals a small but critical part of God’s purposes for events that will happen before eternity begins.

- *he cried out in a loud voice*: Compare {{Job 37:2-5|Job 37:2–5}}; {{Psalm 18:13|Psalm 18:13}}; {{Psalm 29:3-4|Psalm 29:3–4}}.

Revelation shows God's plans for the world but keeps the mystery of his ways. The martyrs did not get an immediate answer to their cries ({{Revelation 6:10|Revelation 6:10}}). The meaning of the seventh seal remains silent ({{Revelation 8:1|Revelation 8:1}}). Here, the seven thunders are kept secret (compare {{Daniel 12:9|Daniel 12:9}}).

- Raising the right hand is common for taking an oath today, but it is rare in the Bible (compare {{Genesis 14:22|Genesis 14:22}}; {{Genesis 24:9|24:9}}; {{Daniel 12:7|Daniel 12:7}}). 

- When making an oath, Jews were careful not to use God’s name lightly (see {{Exodus 20:7|Exodus 20:7}}). Jesus also corrected people who made oaths without sincerity (see {{Matthew 5:33-37|Matthew 5:33–37}}; {{Matthew 23:16-22|23:16–22}}). When God made an oath, he used his own name, because there is no higher authority (see {{Genesis 22:16|Genesis 22:16}}; {{Psalm 89:35-36|Psalm 89:35–36}}; {{Jeremiah 22:5|Jeremiah 22:5}}; {{Hebrews 6:13-18|Hebrews 6:13–18}}).

- *he begins to sound his trumpet*: See {{1 Corinthians 15:51-54|1 Corinthians 15:51–54}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:16|1 Thessalonians 4:16}}. 

- God's mysterious plan for the world is not a surprise. The prophets who served God in the past warned that the day of the Lord would come (see {{Joel 2:1-3|Joel 2:1–3}}, {{Joel 2:10-11|10–11}}; {{Amos 5:18-20|Amos 5:18–20}}; {{Zephaniah 1:14-18|Zephaniah 1:14–18}}).

As in Ezekiel's experience, the scroll tasted sweet in the mouth ({{Ezekiel 3:1-3|Ezekiel 3:1–3}}; see {{Jeremiah 15:16|Jeremiah 15:16}}; see also {{Psalm 19:10|Psalms 19:10}}; {{Psalm 119:103|119:103}}). The future experiences for God's people would be sweet, including the victory of God's plan and the vindication of his people. John's *bitter stomach* is similar to the effects of Ezekiel's tough message for Israel ({{Ezekiel 3:8-9|Ezekiel 3:8–9}}). The process of fulfilling God's plan involves hardship.

Unlike Ezekiel, who prophesied only for Israel, John must prophesy about (or *against*) all the people of the world. There is debate about whether "about" or "against" is the best translation. "About" allows for both promise and judgment (see both in {{Revelation 21:24-27|Revelation 21:24–27}}).

The instructions to measure the temple remind us of Ezekiel’s visions (see {{Ezekiel 40:1-42:20|Ezekiel 40–42}}; {{Ezekiel 43:13-17|43:13–17}}). The Romans destroyed the Jerusalem temple in AD 70. These details symbolize God's precise knowledge and care for his people (compare {{Revelation 7:2-4|Revelation 7:2–4}}; {{Zechariah 2:1-5|Zechariah 2:1–5}}).

- This section shows people choosing to ignore God's call to repent. Attempts to silence his messengers fail, and God wins. 

- Many have tried to identify the two witnesses in this chapter. Moses and Elijah, who appeared with Jesus at the transfiguration ({{Matthew 17:3|Matthew 17:3}}; {{Mark 9:4|Mark 9:4}}; {{Luke 9:30|Luke 9:30}}), are likely candidates (see {{Revelation 11:6|Revelation 11:6}}). They represent the law and the prophets. Others suggest Enoch and Elijah because they did not die (see {{Genesis 5:21-24|Genesis 5:21–24}}; {{2 Kings 2:11-12|2 Kings 2:11–12}}). Some think of Peter and Paul, or James and John. 

More important than their identities is their role in confirming God's message through the testimony of *two or three witnesses* (see {{Deuteronomy 17:6|Deuteronomy 17:6}}). God provides a dual witness to the world about the coming judgment, making it clear that his word will come true ({{Deuteronomy 19:15|Deuteronomy 19:15}}; {{Matthew 18:15-16|Matthew 18:15–16}}).

In the vision, John shared God’s message through an action of prophecy. He measured the temple and the altar. This was like what happened in Ezekiel’s vision recorded in Ezekiel chapter 40. It’s also like what happened in Zechariah’s vision recorded in Zechariah 2:1–2.

Then John told a story like the parables Jesus often told. John told it to show what God would do in the future. Two people were witnesses to God in a city where many evil things happened. Like Moses, the witnesses had power to send plagues. Like Elijah, they had power to keep rain from falling.

John also described the witnesses as lampstands. In Revelation 1:20 lampstands were a sign for the church. Like Jesus, God’s witnesses suffered and were killed for being faithful to God. Then God raised them from the dead. Just like at Jesus’ resurrection, there was an earthquake when this happened. This led the people in the city to give glory to God. This meant that they were humble and recognised God’s authority. It meant that they turned away from worshipping false gods. That hadn’t happened after the plagues from the first four trumpets.

- The outer courtyard of the Jerusalem Temple, which was outside the stone warning fence, was considered the place for the Gentile nations. John uses this image to make a clear distinction between the people God recognizes and those he does not.

- The *42 months* and *1,260 days* represent three and a half years, or an incomplete seven (see study notes on Daniel 7:24–25; 8:26; 9:24–27).
