John frequently uses these time periods in Revelation when persecution is evident and evil seems to control the world. God's people will remain secure in him (see study note on Revelation 11:1) even though God permits evil forces to persecute them (see {{Revelation 13:7|Revelation 13:7}}; {{Mark 10:30|Mark 10:30}}).

- During the period of persecution, God will not abandon the world. He will send two witnesses to announce the coming judgment, similar to how God sent Jonah to Nineveh ({{Jonah 1:2|Jonah 1:2}}; {{Jonah 4:11|4:11}}).

- Burlap clothing symbolized mourning or repentance (see {{Genesis 37:34|Genesis 37:34}}; {{2 Samuel 3:31|2 Samuel 3:31}}; {{Nehemiah 9:1|Nehemiah 9:1}}; {{Esther 4:1|Esther 4:1}}; {{Jonah 3:6|Jonah 3:6}}).
*two olive trees and the two lampstands*: See study note on Revelation 1:12; see also {{Exodus 25:31-40|Exodus 25:31–40}}; {{Zechariah 4:2-6|Zechariah 4:2–6}}.

In one of the psalms, God is described as having fire coming from his mouth, symbolizing judgment on his enemies ({{Psalm 18:8|Psalm 18:8}}; see also {{2 Samuel 22:9|2 Samuel 22:9}}). Compare with Elijah, {{2 Kings 1:1-15|2 Kings 1:1–15}}.

These two witnesses received the power to stop the rain and bring plagues, similar to Elijah (see {{1 Kings 17:1|1 Kings 17:1}}; {{1 Kings 18:41-46|18:41–46}}) and Moses (see {{Exodus 7:14-24|Exodus 7:14–24}}; {{Exodus 8:1-11:10|8:1–11:10}}).

After the witnesses complete their testimony, the scene changes dramatically. The beast (compare {{Revelation 13:1|Revelation 13:1}}) appears for the first time. It is linked to the bottomless pit. Like all enemies of God, the beast fights against God’s witnesses and kills them.

- *Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city*: Evil is so vengeful that it even dishonors the dead. 

- *the great city*: The name “the great city” would have immediately suggested Rome to early readers ({{Revelation 16:19|Revelation 16:19}}; {{Revelation 17:18|17:18}}; {{Revelation 18:10|18:10}}, {{Revelation 18:16|16}}, {{Revelation 18:18-19|18–19}}, {{Revelation 18:21|21}}). However, John also describes it as the city where their Lord was crucified, as well as Sodom and Egypt—all places hostile to God and his people (see also {{Revelation 17:5|Revelation 17:5}}, {{Revelation 17:9|9}}). 

- *where their Lord was also crucified*: There is a direct connection between how evil forces treated the Lord and the experiences of persecuted Christians (see {{Acts 9:5|Acts 9:5}}).

- Leaving people's bodies out for public display was a way to dishonor them after death (see {{1 Samuel 31:10|1 Samuel 31:10}}; the usual Roman custom was to leave bodies hanging after crucifixion). 

- *peoples and tribes and tongues and nations*: This phrase shows that all the peoples of the world are represented in this public display.
*And those … will gloat over them and celebrate*: God's enemies dislike and reject his messengers.

- The death of the two witnesses does not end their mission. God was not defeated in the death of Jesus, and he will not be defeated by the death of his witnesses. The God of resurrection breathed life into the dead, making them stand up (see {{Ezekiel 37:3-5|Ezekiel 37:3–5}}, {{Ezekiel 37:10|10}}), proving God's power. 

- *great fear*: It is frightening for sinful humans to face the power of the living God (see {{Hebrews 10:31|Hebrews 10:31}}).

*they went up to heaven in a cloud*: This event is similar to the way Jesus rose (or ascended) to heaven (see {{Acts 1:9|Acts 1:9}}). It also resembles other ascents found in Scripture (see {{2 Kings 2:11-12|2 Kings 2:11–12}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:17|1 Thessalonians 4:17}}).

- Earthquakes often occur during important events in biblical history (see {{Exodus 19:18|Exodus 19:18}}; {{1 Kings 19:11-12|1 Kings 19:11–12}}; {{Matthew 27:51|Matthew 27:51}}). 

- *Seven thousand*: This number of deaths shows God's role in judgment (contrast {{1 Kings 19:18|1 Kings 19:18}}). 

- *the rest … gave glory to the God of heaven*: Those who survived the earthquake had to recognize God's power and control over the world (see {{Philippians 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9–11}}).
Loud voices in the court of heaven sing a victory song. The earth has become the kingdom of our Lord and his Christ, who reigns as king forever.

When the seventh trumpet was blown, John once again saw heaven and God’s throne.

In Revelation 4:8, the four living creatures worshipped God. They worshipped by saying that God was, and he is, and he will come.

In Revelation 11:17, the elders worshipped God as the one who is and who was. This showed that God had already come. Jesus the Messiah had already come to earth to rule completely.

John was a witness to how this was celebrated in heaven. The temple was opened and the ark of the covenant could be seen. This meant that creation was no longer separated from God. God’s kingdom in heaven had been made one with his rule on earth.

Next John would be shown how God would destroy those who destroy the earth. These were all who refused to accept God’s rule on earth.

The seventh trumpet, also called *the third woe* ({{Revelation 11:14|Revelation 11:14}}; see also {{Revelation 9:12|9:12}}), shows a scene of final judgment and the eternal kingdom. Like in {{Revelation 7:9-17|Revelation 7:9–17}}, this scene offers a dramatic view of the ultimate Christian hope with God. Amidst this picture of judgment, the reader remembers eternity with God.

The twenty-four elders, who represent God's people, confirm that God has taken his place as the victorious King (see study note on Revelation 4:4). Their worship recognizes God’s sovereign rule as the Almighty (see {{Revelation 4:10-11|Revelation 4:10–11}}; {{Revelation 5:8-10|5:8–10}}).

The thanksgiving prayer describes God as the one who is and who always was. The phrase *is to come* (see {{Revelation 1:4|Revelation 1:4}}, {{Revelation 1:8|8}}) no longer applies. In this scene, eternity has arrived, and God has begun to reign.

- The nations were angry when they did not follow God's commands (see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}). But now, things will change because God's anger has arrived. God will reward his holy people (see {{Revelation 22:12|Revelation 22:12}}) with new life as his children (see {{John 1:12|John 1:12}}; {{John 20:31|20:31}}). 

- *fear Your name*: God's name represents his nature; fearing God's name means accepting who he is (see “Fear of the Lord” Theme Note). 

- The end of the age will be the time to destroy those who have not accepted God's love (see {{John 3:16-20|John 3:16–20}}). They will go into the lake of fire ({{Revelation 20:15|Revelation 20:15}}). This fate of God's enemies is the third and final terror ({{Revelation 11:14|Revelation 11:14}}).

- This verse dramatically concludes the first half of Revelation and connects to the second half. 

- In this scene, the temple and the ark symbolize God's presence. The earthly ark was a copy of the heavenly ark's design (see {{Exodus 25:40|Exodus 25:40}}; {{Hebrews 8:5|Hebrews 8:5}}).

The number twelve suggests that the woman represents God's people (compare {{Revelation 12:15-17|Revelation 12:15–17}}; see {{Jeremiah 2:32|Jeremiah 2:32}}; {{2 Corinthians 11:2|2 Corinthians 11:2}}; {{Ephesians 5:32|Ephesians 5:32}}), from whom the Messiah came. This woman is marked by God's glory, unlike the prostitute (see {{Revelation 17:1-6|Revelation 17:1–6}}), who faces destruction.

John recorded a story about a woman, her child and a dragon. He made it clear that they were signs.

The woman was a sign for the people of Israel. Jesus came from the people of Israel. He was the son that John saw born in the vision.

The woman was also a sign for the church. Jesus’ followers were the rest of her children.

The dragon was the devil. The dragon tried to kill Jesus to stop God’s plan. But Jesus was taken up to God and to his throne.

Then in heaven Michael and other angels fought against the dragon and his angels. The dragon was thrown out of heaven down to earth. He chased the woman and tried to harm her children.

This story was a way to talk about victory over sin, death and evil. Jesus was raised from the dead and returned to heaven. That was how he won this victory. It showed that Jesus had power over the devil in heaven and on earth.

Jesus’ followers share in Jesus’ victory over sin, death and evil. They have victory by believing in Jesus and sharing the good news with others. They face suffering for following Jesus faithfully. That is what was meant by the dragon chasing the woman’s children. But God provides the help they need.

Satan is shown as a dragon. He plots to oppose God's plans but fails. After losing a direct battle with God and Christ, he tries to harm God's followers. Three short scenes summarize the story ({{Revelation 12:1-6|Revelation 12:1–6}}), followed by details of the war in heaven ({{Revelation 12:7-9|12:7–9}}) and the war on earth ({{Revelation 12:13-17|12:13–17}}).

The people of God are pictured as a woman who gives birth to the Messiah. Even though the devil has already been defeated, he continues to attack her and her children ({{Revelation 12:1-17|Revelation 12:1–17}}). With his two followers, the beast and the false prophet, Satan tries to keep controlling the world ({{Revelation 13:1-18|Revelation 13:1–18}}) before the final battle with the Lord ({{Revelation 14:1-20|14:1–20}}).

The symbolic woman experiencing the pain of labor represents Christ’s birth. This reflects the biblical theme of Israel’s struggle while waiting for deliverance (see {{Isaiah 26:16-18|Isaiah 26:16–18}}; {{Jeremiah 4:31|Jeremiah 4:31}}; {{Micah 4:9-10|Micah 4:9–10}}; {{John 16:21|John 16:21}}).

- The large red dragon symbolizes Satan (see {{Revelation 12:9|Revelation 12:9}}). 

- *seven heads, ten horns*: These numbers symbolize a mix of divine and created powers (see {{Revelation 17:7-14|Revelation 17:7–14}}). 

- The historic battle between evil and God's people occurs on a cosmic scale (see {{Genesis 3:1-7|Genesis 3:1–7}}, {{Genesis 3:14-15|14–15}}; {{Job 1:9-12|Job 1:9–12}}). 

- Herod’s wish to kill Jesus showed Satan’s attempt to destroy her baby after birth (see {{Matthew 2:7-8|Matthew 2:7–8}}, {{Matthew 2:16|16}}).

- Jesus was the son who was to rule all nations (see {{Luke 1:31-33|Luke 1:31–33}}; {{Luke 2:30-32|2:30–32}}; compare {{Psalm 2:6-12|Psalm 2:6–12}}). 

- Although agents of evil killed Jesus, God saved him from the dragon and raised him from the dead ({{Matthew 28:6|Matthew 28:6}}; {{Mark 10:33-34|Mark 10:33–34}}; {{Mark 16:6|16:6}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:3-4|1 Corinthians 15:3–4}}). This scene summarizes the life of Jesus on earth, from his birth to his death and resurrection. 

- *caught up to God and to His throne*: See {{Acts 1:9-11|Acts 1:9–11}}.

- Like the people of Israel who were spiritually refined in the wilderness (see {{Hosea 2:14-15|Hosea 2:14–15}}; {{Acts 7:38-45|Acts 7:38–45}}) and in exile in Babylon (see {{Isaiah 5:13|Isaiah 5:13}}; {{Ezekiel 12:1-3|Ezekiel 12:1–3}}), the Christian church must face its own challenges. Revelation shares messages of endurance and perseverance during difficult times and shows that God provides places of refuge and ways to escape for his people (compare {{1 Corinthians 10:13|1 Corinthians 10:13}}). 

- *1,260 days*: See study note on Revelation 11:2–3.

- This scene reveals the dragon’s identity and power. 

- God sends Michael, the warrior archangel (see {{Daniel 12:1|Daniel 12:1}}; {{Jude 9|Jude 1:9}}), to face the dragon and his angels. God does not need to fight the battle himself (see {{Matthew 26:53|Matthew 26:53}}), and Satan is defeated.
Satan's defeat encourages Christians who, like those in Revelation, do not fear death (see {{John 12:24-26|John 12:24–26}}).
*when the dragon saw*: The scene continues from {{Revelation 12:9|Revelation 12:9}}.

- *two wings of a great eagle* (see {{Exodus 19:4-6|Exodus 19:4–6}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:10-11|Deuteronomy 32:10–11}}; {{Isaiah 40:29-31|Isaiah 40:29–31}}): God strengthens his people but does not promise they will avoid persecution or death. 

- *a time, and times, and half a time*: This is usually understood as three and a half years (see {{Revelation 11:2-3|Revelation 11:2–3}}).

John imagines Satan as Leviathan, a great sea monster (compare {{Job 41:1|Job 41:1}}), trying to destroy God's people (the woman; see study note on Revelation 12:1). In the vision, the earth protects the woman, and the dangerous waters are held back. This is similar to the way God contained the waters of chaos at creation (compare {{Genesis 1:2|Genesis 1:2}}, {{Genesis 1:6-7|6–7}}, {{Genesis 1:9-10|9–10}}).
The dragon becomes hostile towards the woman's children, who are believers. They follow God's commandments and continue to testify about Jesus.
*on the shore of the sea*: By contrast, the lamb stands on the rock of Zion ({{Revelation 12:17|Revelation 12:17}}).

John shows that the dragon carries out his war ({{Revelation 12:17|Revelation 12:17}}) through two beasts. Together with Satan, these three form an evil trinity, meaning three evil beings acting together as one group.

The beast comes out of the sea, symbolizing evil. Like the dragon, it has seven heads and ten horns (see {{Revelation 12:3|Revelation 12:3}}). The crowns show its political and military power (compare {{Revelation 17:3|Revelation 17:3}}, {{Revelation 17:7-11|7–11}}; {{Daniel 7:7|Daniel 7:7}}, {{Daniel 7:19-20|19–20}}) and indicate that Satan leads this beast's empire.
The first beast is the second member of the evil trinity (see study note on Revelation 12:18–13:18). It likely represents Roman power (see “Four World Empires” Theme Note).

In the vision, John saw a beast come out of the sea. He saw another beast come out of the earth. They were like the four animals Daniel saw in a vision recorded in Daniel chapter 7.

In Daniel’s vision, beasts were signs of human governments. Thrones were signs of authority and horns were signs of power. This was true for John’s vision as well. The first beast was a sign of a powerful ruler or government. The second beast was a sign of a person or group that supported them.

In Revelation 16:13 the second beast was also called a false prophet. The devil was the dragon who gave these beasts power over people. The first beast was allowed to rule for 42 months. The second beast made people worship the first beast and be marked in a certain way.

This was the opposite of when God’s servants were marked by God’s seal. The mark of the beast from the sea was the number 666. All of this was like something happening in John’s time in the lands controlled by Rome.

Authorities and rulers made people obey and worship Rome and the emperor. Those who refused to worship the Roman ruler Caesar were treated badly or killed.
Satan turns the beast into a false god by giving it his power, throne, and authority. In the first century, Roman emperors often claimed to be gods.

- Satan often imitates God. Here, the beast copies the death and resurrection of Jesus. 

- One of the beast’s heads appears to have been fatally wounded but then healed. This detail has led many interpreters to connect the beast with the Roman emperor Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68. A tradition developed that Nero was so evil that he either did not really die or would return as another tyrant like Domitian, who ruled from AD 81 to 96. In {{Revelation 17:9-10|Revelation 17:9–10}}, the beast’s seven heads are linked to both *seven hills* (Rome) and *seven kings.*
The forty-two months represent three and a half years of persecution and evil rule (see study note on Revelation 11:2–3).

The four characteristics of the beast are:

- he speaks against God,

- he holds power for a short time,

- he fights against God's people, and

- he governs the world.

However, God remains in control.
The beast has power over all the people in the world.
People who worshiped the beast received its mark ({{Revelation 13:15-17|Revelation 13:15–17}}) and are not in the *Book of Life* (see {{Revelation 20:12|20:12}}).

The scene ({{Revelation 13:1-10|Revelation 13:1–10}}) ends with a dramatic conclusion similar to {{Jeremiah 15:2|Jeremiah 15:2}}; {{Jeremiah 43:11|43:11}}. Anyone who can hear must listen, because judgment is coming (compare {{Revelation 2:7|Revelation 2:7}}, {{Revelation 2:11|11}}, {{Revelation 2:17|17}}).
God's holy people are called to stay strong and faithful during temporary persecution.

- The beast appears as a lamb, the same symbol used for Christ (see {{Revelation 5:6-13|Revelation 5:6–13}}; {{Revelation 7:9-17|7:9–17}}; {{Revelation 14:1-4|14:1–4}}), but this lamb spoke like a dragon. This image represents a false messiah. 

- The two horns might symbolize two emperors, possibly Nero and Domitian.

*another beast*: This second beast, the third member of the evil trinity (see study note on Revelation 12:18–13:18), is later called the *false prophet* ({{Revelation 16:13|16:13}}). As a high priest of false religion, he leads the world to worship the first beast and the dragon (see also {{Revelation 16:13-14|16:13–14}}).

- *caused the earth … to worship the first beast*: Rome under the rule of the emperor demanded that people worship Emperor Domitian. 

- *whose mortal wound had been healed*: This description might point to Domitian, who many believed was a return, or reincarnation, of Nero (see study note on Revelation 13:3). The image represents the constant return of evil, especially in the last days (see study note on Revelation 17:8).
The second beast gets its power from the first beast, which follows the dragon ({{Revelation 13:4|Revelation 13:4}}).

In New Testament times, false prophets amazed people with stories of divine visits and idols speaking for the gods they represented (see {{Acts 16:16-18|Acts 16:16–18}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:2-3|1 Corinthians 12:2–3}}). These practices involved worshiping demons (see {{1 Corinthians 10:20-21|1 Corinthians 10:20–21}}) and were highlighted in the Roman emperor cult. Those who refused to follow were executed.
*it was given … was permitted*: God never gives up ultimate authority. These evil creatures can rebel against God, but they are not in control.

- *small and great, rich and poor, free and slave*: Everyone must accept the beast's evil mark of ownership (see {{Revelation 14:9|Revelation 14:9}}, {{Revelation 14:11|11}}; {{Revelation 19:20|19:20}}; {{Revelation 20:4|20:4}}). This mark is needed to buy or sell. The text does not clearly describe what the mark is or how it looks. 

- On the right hand or forehead suggests the branding of slaves, showing the beast owns them. 

- *the name of the beast or the number of its name*: In both Hebrew and Greek, letters of the alphabet stand for numbers, giving names a numerical value ({{Revelation 13:18|Revelation 13:18}}).

- *a call for wisdom*: John gives a clue to help his readers understand the meaning of the beast’s number. 

- *of a man*: John hides the man’s identity, possibly to protect himself and his readers from danger (compare the use of Babylon as a symbol for Rome, {{Revelation 17:9|Revelation 17:9}}). 

- The number 666 represents supernatural evil (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note). John might have used the transliteration *Caesar Neron* (a Hebrew spelling of the name) to reach the number 666. Later scribes, who spoke Greek but not Hebrew, changed the number to *616* in some manuscripts, likely to match the name’s numerical value in Greek.

- *standing*: See {{Revelation 5:6|Revelation 5:6}}; study note on Revelation 12:18. 

- *144,000*: God’s righteous remnant (see study note on Revelation 7:4–8). 

- The mark on their foreheads (contrast {{Revelation 13:16-17|Revelation 13:16–17}}) is the name of both the lamb and his father, showing the unity of Jesus and the Father (see {{John 5:20-23|John 5:20–23}}; {{John 14:5-10|14:5–10}}; {{John 17:22|17:22}}).

John described the Lamb in ways that Psalm 2 described a certain king. This was the king that God chose to be the son of God.

Other kings, nations and rulers on earth tried to be more powerful than God. But God’s son ruled from Mount Zion as king over all other rulers. Mount Zion was another name for Mount Moriah.

The Lamb that John saw standing on Mount Zion was this king from Psalm 2. The two beasts in Revelation chapter 13 were like the rulers that opposed God in Psalm 2. The Lamb was joined by his faithful followers. They worshipped him with a new song. This was a way to celebrate Jesus’ work of rescuing them from evil.

Being marked with Jesus’ name and the Father’s name showed that they belonged to Jesus. John had seen the crowd of 144,000 people before. They were a sign of all the people throughout history who are God’s faithful people. That’s what it meant that they were a first offering.
The true lamb and his followers are very different from the evil trinity.

This great choir sang a new song that only those redeemed from the earth could learn. These people had died and were already with the Lord. This might explain why John did not include the content of their refrain for readers still facing life's challenges (compare {{2 Corinthians 12:4|2 Corinthians 12:4}}).

- These warriors were ceremonially pure (*not … defiled*) and morally blameless. 

- *for they are virgins*: Referring to men as *virgins* is a metaphor for the faithfulness of God’s people. The image might refer to the church as the virgin bride of Christ (see {{2 Corinthians 11:2|2 Corinthians 11:2}}; {{Ephesians 5:25-27|Ephesians 5:25–27}}). It also suggests that the church members are like soldiers in a holy war who must abstain from sexual intercourse (see {{Deuteronomy 23:9-10|Deuteronomy 23:9–10}}; {{1 Samuel 21:5|1 Samuel 21:5}}). 

- These faithful people are a special offering, literally called *firstfruits* (see {{Exodus 13:14-16|Exodus 13:14–16}}; {{Exodus 23:19|23:19}}; {{Leviticus 23:9-14|Leviticus 23:9–14}}; {{Numbers 3:40-51|Numbers 3:40–51}}; {{Numbers 18:15-20|18:15–20}}; {{Luke 2:22-24|Luke 2:22–24}}), who have been purchased for God. 

- *no lie was found in their mouths*: John teaches that liars will never enter heaven ({{Revelation 21:8|Revelation 21:8}}, {{Revelation 21:27|27}}; {{Revelation 22:15|22:15}}; see also {{John 8:44|John 8:44}}). The followers of Jesus speak and live the truth (see also {{John 8:32|John 8:32}}; {{John 14:6|14:6}}).
The first angel announces the eternal good news. This includes the message that God will judge soon. It is a final call to repent.

The first angel John saw made an announcement to everyone on earth. God is the Creator and is the only one who should be worshipped. He is going to judge the world. That message was good news for people.

The second angel announced that Babylon had fallen. This meant that Babylon had lost all its power. God judged Babylon for not accepting the good news that the first angel announced. He also judged Babylon for causing other nations to sin.

The third angel warned about judgement against all who followed and worshipped the beast. This was the beast that came out of the sea in Revelation chapter 13. Both the beast and Babylon were signs for human governments that seek complete power. These governments treat those who are faithful to Jesus badly. In John’s time, that government was Rome. John’s vision offered comfort to God’s people who were being treated unfairly. They would be blessed even if they were put to death. The Holy Spirit would give them rest.
Three angels fly through the sky carrying messages from God.

Babylon likely symbolizes Rome (see {{Revelation 16:19|Revelation 16:19}}; {{Revelation 17:5-9|17:5–9}}). It represents earthly power and corruption. God's arrival as judge ({{Revelation 14:7|Revelation 14:7}}) signifies the end of earthly powers.

- The third angel announces God's judgment ({{Revelation 14:7|Revelation 14:7}}) on the false worship of the beast and his statue (see {{Revelation 13:12-18|Revelation 13:12–18}}; {{Revelation 19:20|19:20}}; {{Revelation 20:4|20:4}}). God responds to the rebellion against his rule with anger, shown as a cup of bitter wine (see {{Revelation 16:1-21|Revelation 16}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}). 

- *fire and sulfur … smoke*: This description of judgment (see also {{Revelation 19:20|Revelation 19:20}}; {{Revelation 20:10|20:10}}, {{Revelation 20:14-15|14–15}}) reminds us of God's judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah ({{Genesis 18:16-19:28|Genesis 18:16–19:28}}). 

- Those condemned to a fiery end will suffer in the presence of the holy angels and the Lamb (compare {{Luke 16:22-24|Luke 16:22–24}}).

Christians who first read this letter faced real threats of persecution and death. John urges God's people to obey and stay faithful (see {{Revelation 2:10|Revelation 2:10}}; {{Revelation 3:10|3:10}}; {{Revelation 12:17|12:17}}; {{Revelation 13:10|13:10}}).

- A powerful voice from heaven tells John to write again (see {{Revelation 1:11|Revelation 1:11}}, {{Revelation 1:19|19}}; {{Revelation 21:5|21:5}}; compare {{Revelation 10:4|10:4}}). 

- *Blessed are … those who die in the Lord*: God wants those who suffer persecution to be with him and enjoy his blessings and rest. 

- Mentioning hard work and good deeds with eternal reward hints at rewards given based on actions ({{Revelation 20:12|Revelation 20:12}}).

- *the Son of Man*: Or *like a son of man;* see study note on Revelation 1:13. 

- A gold crown symbolizes status or power, clearly distinguishing Jesus from the angels (see {{Revelation 4:4|Revelation 4:4}}; {{Revelation 6:2|6:2}}; {{Revelation 9:7|9:7}}; {{Revelation 12:3|12:3}}; {{Revelation 13:1|13:1}}). 

- The sharp sickle symbolizes God's harvest of judgment (see {{Revelation 14:17-18|Revelation 14:17–18}}; see also {{Jeremiah 51:33|Jeremiah 51:33}}; {{Hosea 6:11|Hosea 6:11}}; {{Micah 4:12-13|Micah 4:12–13}}).

In Matthew 9:37–38 and John 4:35–38 Jesus had talked about the world as a harvest field. This meant that people were ready to believe in him and follow him.

In John’s vision, John saw Jesus harvest the earth’s corn. This was a picture of Jesus saving those who belong to him. John also saw an angel harvest the earth’s grapes. This could be a picture of God’s anger and judgement against those who do evil. It could also be a picture of God’s people who were put to death. Their blood was spilled as they laboured to follow Jesus faithfully.
Two short scenes show God's judgment.
The temple and the altar symbolize God's presence (see {{Revelation 9:13|Revelation 9:13}}; {{Revelation 11:19|11:19}}; {{Revelation 16:7|16:7}}).

- The ripe grapes (see {{Amos 8:2|Amos 8:2}}) trampled in the winepress highlight God's power to judge (see {{Revelation 19:15|Revelation 19:15}}; {{Joel 3:13|Joel 3:13}}). 

- People built winepresses outside cities and towns; here, the city is Jerusalem. The bloody river of death stretched about 290 kilometers (180 miles). This shows that God’s enemies have no chance when the Son of Man comes in judgment. This destruction is closely linked with the final battle in {{Revelation 19:17-21|Revelation 19:17–21}}. God is just and fair in giving people exactly what they deserve (see {{Revelation 16:5-7|Revelation 16:5–7}}).

This series of seven final plagues ({{Revelation 15:1-16:21|Revelation 15:1–16:21}}) completes God's punishment of his enemies (see {{Revelation 16:17|16:17}}; {{Amos 1:1-2:16|Amos 1–2}}; {{Romans 1:18-2:16|Romans 1:18–2:16}}). Revelation revisits the topic of God's punishment later ({{Revelation 19:15-21|Revelation 19:15–21}}).

In Revelation 14:12, John had described God’s people. They obeyed God, were faithful to Jesus and were patient.

In Revelation chapter 15, John saw them celebrating what they had been waiting for. They had been patiently waiting for God to rule completely over all things. God had freed them from the power of the beast. They sang praises to God for being the fair ruler who does what is right.

Their song was like Moses’ song in Exodus chapter 15. Moses had praised God for freeing the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. In Moses’ song, other nations were afraid when they saw what God did. In the song of God’s people, other nations worshipped God. They worshipped him because they saw that he did what was right. Doing what was right included stopping everything that was wrong, sinful and evil.

This song was sung as the angels prepared the last seven plagues. These plagues were a sign of how God would finish judging the world.

The third and final cycle of seven judgments (see study note on Revelation 6:1–16:21) begins with a vision of God's victorious people singing a hymn of praise ({{Revelation 15:2-4|Revelation 15:2–4}}). Then, a scene of the temple appears ({{Revelation 15:5-8|Revelation 15:5–8}}), where angels come out carrying the bowls of God's judgment for the earth ({{Revelation 16:1-21|16:1–21}}).

The glass sea mixed with fire symbolizes victory through testing. Those who defeated the beast (see {{Revelation 13:1-8|Revelation 13:1–8}}, {{Revelation 13:15-18|15–18}}) hold harps that represent ultimate peace. Their position on the *sea of glass* (compare {{Revelation 4:6|Revelation 4:6}}) symbolizes their endurance through the *fire* of persecution (compare {{Psalm 66:12|Psalm 66:12}}; {{Isaiah 43:2|Isaiah 43:2}}; {{Daniel 3:8-30|Daniel 3:8–30}}).

- *O Lord God Almighty!* (see also {{Revelation 1:8|Revelation 1:8}}; {{Revelation 4:8|4:8}}; {{Revelation 11:17|11:17}}; {{Revelation 16:7|16:7}}; {{Revelation 19:6|19:6}}; {{Revelation 21:22|21:22}}): For persecuted Christians, knowing that God is all-powerful brings comfort and security. 

- The fact that God is just and true supports human integrity in a confused, unjust, and dishonest world. 

- God is the supreme, universal King of the nations, not a local deity tied to one nation or a human ruler with limited power.

The song of Moses and the Lamb shows that God’s purposes in the old covenant (God’s earlier promise and relationship with his people) and the new covenant (his promise through Jesus) are united and work together.

- *Who will not fear … and glorify Your name?*: This rhetorical question (see {{Jeremiah 10:7|Jeremiah 10:7}}) suggests that only a fool would fail to do so (see {{Revelation 14:7|Revelation 14:7}}; {{Revelation 16:9|16:9}}; {{Psalm 14:1|Psalms 14:1}}; {{Psalm 53:1|53:1}}). 

- *You alone are holy*: See {{Revelation 16:5|Revelation 16:5}}; {{Leviticus 11:44|Leviticus 11:44}}; {{1 Peter 1:16|1 Peter 1:16}}. God's holiness is the reason for our worship and salvation. 

- *All nations will come and worship*: Some will be forced to acknowledge God (compare {{Philippians 2:10-11|Philippians 2:10–11}}), but all will recognize that God's deeds and judgments are revealed, righteous, and just.

- God's tabernacle shows God's presence (see {{John 1:14|John 1:14}}). Even the plagues come from God's presence. Christ's sacrifice ({{Matthew 27:51|Matthew 27:51}}; {{Mark 15:38|Mark 15:38}}; {{Hebrews 6:19-20|Hebrews 6:19–20}}; {{Hebrews 10:19-20|10:19–20}}) removed the barrier between God and humanity (see {{Exodus 26:31-35|Exodus 26:31–35}}; {{Leviticus 16:1-34|Leviticus 16}}). Now, those who do not belong to Christ feel the full impact of God's presence (see {{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15}}; {{Isaiah 13:4-12|Isaiah 13:4–12}}; {{Zephaniah 2:1-3|Zephaniah 2:1–3}}; {{Malachi 3:2-3|Malachi 3:2–3}}). 

- *bright linen*: Linen, a symbol of purity, was also worn by priests during their duties (see {{Exodus 28:39-43|Exodus 28:39–43}}; {{Leviticus 16:4|Leviticus 16:4}}, {{Leviticus 16:23|23}}; see also {{Ezekiel 9:2-3|Ezekiel 9:2–3}}; {{Daniel 12:6-7|Daniel 12:6–7}}). These angels do not intercede; they are agents of judgment. The linen represents the purity and justice of God's judgment. 

- The gold sashes across their chests likely symbolize their divine mission as ministers of justice for God (compare {{Revelation 1:13|Revelation 1:13}}).

- *the four living creatures*: See {{Revelation 4:6-8|Revelation 4:6–8}}. 

- *seven golden bowls*: These bowls are likely similar to the offering pans used in ancient worship (see {{Exodus 37:16|Exodus 37:16}}).
Smoke filled the temple to show God's glory and power ({{Isaiah 6:4|Isaiah 6:4}}; see {{Exodus 19:16-18|Exodus 19:16–18}}; {{Exodus 40:34-35|40:34–35}}; {{1 Kings 8:10-13|1 Kings 8:10–13}}).

The powerful voice likely belongs to God (also in {{Revelation 6:6|Revelation 6:6}}; {{Revelation 9:13|9:13}}; {{Revelation 16:17|16:17}}; {{Revelation 18:4|18:4}}; {{Revelation 19:5|19:5}}; see {{Isaiah 66:6|Isaiah 66:6}}).

The seven bowls of God’s anger were signs of God’s final judgements. The first four bowls brought judgement against people who refused to give God glory. An angel praised God for judging fairly. God was finally punishing those who put his people to death. This is what the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9–11 had been waiting for.

The last three bowls brought judgement against the beast and the nations that followed it. As John described these things, he recorded a message from Jesus. Jesus reminded believers to pay attention and to be ready for him to come. He didn’t want his followers to be tricked by evil spirits into following the beast. These evil spiritual beings looked like frogs to John.

The judgement against the beast came through splitting its kingdom apart. Those who followed the beast didn’t repent and turn to God. They continued to speak evil things against God. The nations gathered for a war. John didn’t record a battle. Instead, God declared that his plan had been accomplished with the seventh bowl.

The bowls were the third set of sevens in John’s visions. God’s judgements had started with the seven seals. They had continued with the seven trumpets. With the seven bowls an angel announced that God’s judgement was done.

These seven bowls filled with God's wrath symbolize the final judgments on the world. With the seventh bowl, a voice from God's throne shouts, *It is done!* ({{Revelation 16:17|Revelation 16:17}}; compare {{John 19:30|John 19:30}}).

- The harmful sores remind us of the sixth plague in Egypt ({{Exodus 9:9-11|Exodus 9:9–11}}). 

- *mark of the beast*: See {{Revelation 13:13-17|Revelation 13:13–17}}; {{Revelation 14:9-10|14:9–10}}.

The plagues of the second and third bowls are similar to the first plague of Egypt ({{Exodus 7:17-21|Exodus 7:17–21}}). John may have thought about how much of Rome’s food and wealth came from the sea. After Julius Caesar cleared the sea of pirates, shipping became vital for Rome. Its end would mean economic collapse for the empire (see {{Revelation 18:17-19|Revelation 18:17–19}}).

*the angel of the waters*: In Scripture, angels and archangels are shown to have special roles within the order of heaven (see {{Daniel 8:16|Daniel 8:16}}; {{Daniel 9:21|9:21}}; {{Daniel 10:13|10:13}}, {{Daniel 10:21|21}}; {{Daniel 12:1|12:1}}; {{Luke 1:19|Luke 1:19}}, {{Luke 1:26|26}}; see also *1 Enoch* 66:1–2). This angel confirms that these judgments come from God, who is just and holy.

Punishing God's enemies is fair because they killed God's holy people and prophets. Since they shed blood, they must drink blood. The principle of *lex talionis* (the law of retribution), which is the basis of Roman and Jewish law, shows that God is completely fair in judging and rewarding people based on their actions (see {{Revelation 2:23|Revelation 2:23}}; {{Revelation 11:18|11:18}}; {{Revelation 14:13|14:13}}; {{Revelation 18:6|18:6}}; {{Revelation 20:12|20:12}}, {{Revelation 20:13|13}}; {{Revelation 22:12|22:12}}).

*I heard the altar reply*: The response to the angel’s proclamation ({{Revelation 16:5-6|Revelation 16:5–6}}) confirms God’s authority and justice. This praise during judgment reminds persecuted Christians that God cares about his suffering servants and fulfills his purpose in everything.

- The fourth bowl is different from the plagues of Egypt, earlier seals, or trumpets. 

- *the people were scorched*: Contrast {{Revelation 7:16|Revelation 7:16}}. Yet those who faced this judgment refused to repent or honor God (see {{Revelation 9:20-21|Revelation 9:20–21}}; {{Revelation 16:11|16:11}}; compare {{Revelation 14:6-7|14:6–7}}); they even cursed God's name.

- *the throne of the beast*: John might be referring to Rome, the political power of his time. Built on seven hills ({{Revelation 17:9|Revelation 17:9}}), Rome's empire stretched across the sea ({{Revelation 13:1|13:1}}) and dominated the world ({{Revelation 13:7|13:7}}). 

- *plunged into darkness*: This is similar to the ninth plague of Egypt ({{Exodus 10:22|Exodus 10:22}}) and the fourth trumpet ({{Revelation 8:12|Revelation 8:12}}).

- *gnaw their tongues. … curse the God of heaven*: Pain and anger caused these reactions to punishment (compare {{Matthew 8:12|Matthew 8:12}}; {{Matthew 13:42|13:42}}, {{Matthew 13:50|50}}; {{Matthew 22:13|22:13}}; {{Matthew 24:51|24:51}}; {{Matthew 25:30|25:30}}; {{Luke 13:28|Luke 13:28}}).

The Euphrates, the largest river in Mesopotamia, lay between Babylon and Israel. It marked the eastern border of the Roman Empire. If it dried up, kings from the east could move their armies westward (compare {{Revelation 9:13-16|Revelation 9:13–16}}). From John's perspective as an ancient Jewish writer, people would always associate these armies with Mesopotamia, not with countries farther east like China or India.

Three deceitful agents, evil spirits in the form of frogs, symbolize the demonic role of the evil trinity. Although evil powers fight against the Lord, God the Almighty, not any evil power, remains in control.

Readers are warned to stay alert because the Lord will come as unexpectedly as a thief (see also {{Revelation 3:3|Revelation 3:3}}; {{Matthew 24:43|Matthew 24:43}}; {{Matthew 25:13|25:13}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:2|1 Thessalonians 5:2}}; {{2 Peter 3:10|2 Peter 3:10}}). Being ready for his coming requires preparation. Those who are not prepared will lack proper clothing and will find themselves exposed (see {{Matthew 22:11-13|Matthew 22:11–13}}). This imagery refers to two failing churches: 

- lifeless Sardis, which is told to “wake up” ({{Revelation 3:2|Revelation 3:2}}), and

- lukewarm Laodicea, which is advised to get proper clothing ({{Revelation 3:18|Revelation 3:18}}).

The name Armageddon (or *Harmagedon*) likely comes from the Hebrew words *har* (which means “mountain” or “hill”) and Megiddo. Solomon fortified Megiddo along with Gezer in the south and Hazor in the north ({{1 Kings 9:15|1 Kings 9:15}}). The fortress of Megiddo stood on a hill in the largest pass through the Carmel range, strategically guarding the Jezreel Valley. 

The city was on the Via Maris, the main highway between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Many armies used this route, making the site known for bloody battles. For example, Pharaoh Neco killed Josiah here on his way to fight the Assyrians ({{2 Kings 23:29|2 Kings 23:29}}). Armageddon became a symbol for the final conflict between God and the forces of evil.

When the seventh bowl is poured out, something unexpected happens. God's enemies gather for battle. But at the crucial moment, instead of a battle, there is a shout: *It is done!* Jesus spoke these same words from the cross when he completed his work ({{John 19:30|John 19:30}}). No one can ultimately fight against God. This scene shows the end of rebellion against God. What follows are different descriptions of the end.

This judgment scene repeats the events showing the world's destruction ({{Revelation 6:12-14|Revelation 6:12–14}}; {{Revelation 11:13|11:13}}). It also hints at the final judgment ({{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15}}) when the earth will be taken apart to allow for a new creation ({{Revelation 21:1|21:1}}; compare {{Isaiah 45:2|Isaiah 45:2}}; {{Romans 8:19-22|Romans 8:19–22}}).

- Despite the severity of these plagues, people around the world cursed God instead of understanding his reasons for the judgments (see {{Revelation 9:20|Revelation 9:20}}; {{Revelation 16:9|16:9}}, {{Revelation 16:11|11}}). 

- The terrible hailstorm reminds us of the seventh plague on Egypt ({{Exodus 9:23-24|Exodus 9:23–24}}).

One of the angels who carry out God’s judgment speaks to John and calls him to a new scene. In this scene, John sees the coming judgment of the great prostitute, who rules over many waters. 

Rome, which stood on the Tiber River, controlled major centers of power and the water trade routes across the Mediterranean world. Its influence reached from the British Isles to the Euphrates River.

The third vision John wrote about occurred in a desert. The vision was of a woman sitting on a beast. This vision described more about what happened before God’s judgement was finished in Revelation 16:17.

The woman was a prostitute and was a sign for the city of Babylon. Babylon was a sign for the government of Rome. The power behind Babylon came from the beast. This was the same beast that John saw come out of the sea in Revelation chapter 13.

This vision uncovered the evil practices of powerful groups and governments like Babylon. They appear fancy, rich and successful. They have a lot of authority on earth. Yet their power is based on doing evil deeds. They put to death those who oppose them. This includes Jesus’ followers.

The angel explained to John that Babylon’s power wouldn’t last for ever. Rulers who used to support Babylon would destroy it.

The main drama in this section shows the powers that stand against God and cause the persecution and suffering of God’s people. Rome’s power attracted and impressed many people ({{Revelation 17:6|Revelation 17:6}}). John clearly describes Rome's sins and shares God's judgment ({{Revelation 17:3-18|Revelation 17:3–18}}) before he describes Rome’s fall ({{Revelation 18:1-24|18:1–24}}) and heaven’s response to that fall ({{Revelation 19:1-10|19:1–10}}).

- *immoral with her*: This is a biblical image for worshiping other gods (see, for example, {{Exodus 34:12-16|Exodus 34:12–16}}; {{Judges 2:17|Judges 2:17}}; {{Hosea 2:1-23|Hosea 2}}). 

- *intoxicated with … her immorality*: In Scripture, drunkenness often represents nations that engage in reckless and immoral behavior (see {{Revelation 18:3|Revelation 18:3}}, {{Revelation 18:9|9}}; {{Jeremiah 25:27|Jeremiah 25:27}}; {{Jeremiah 51:7|51:7}}; {{Lamentations 4:21|Lamentations 4:21}}; {{Ezekiel 23:33|Ezekiel 23:33}}).

- John is taken in the spirit into the wilderness, which he uses to describe a visionary experience (see {{Revelation 1:10|Revelation 1:10}}; {{Revelation 4:2|4:2}}). He sees a representation of Rome's moral decay and extreme luxury (see {{Revelation 18:12-13|Revelation 18:12–13}}, {{Revelation 18:16|16}}). This shows how such wealth can be offensive to God. 

- The beast here resembles the second figure in the evil trinity (see {{Revelation 13:1-4|Revelation 13:1–4}}). 

- *blasphemous names*: See {{Revelation 13:5-6|Revelation 13:5–6}}. 

- *purple and scarlet*: Clothing in these colors signified royalty and immorality, respectively. 

- *a golden cup*: See {{Jeremiah 51:7|Jeremiah 51:7}}.

In symbolic language, John likely referred to Rome (see {{Revelation 17:9|Revelation 17:9}}) as *BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES*. Babylon symbolized the world's idolatries and evil acts. As the *MOTHER*, she produced followers who imitated her behavior. Rome, like Babylon, worshipped false gods and led other nations into unfaithfulness and idol worship.
God’s holy people were witnesses for Jesus, even shedding their blood (see {{Revelation 16:6|Revelation 16:6}}; {{Hebrews 12:4|Hebrews 12:4}}). During John's time, Rome caused this persecution.
The angel helps John understand the mystery in response to his amazement ({{Revelation 17:8-14|Revelation 17:8–14}}).

- *The beast … it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up*: When Domitian was emperor, from AD 81 to 96, he was as evil as Nero. Both fiercely persecuted the church. Many believed Domitian embodied Nero’s spirit or was Nero himself. This is similar to how people thought John the Baptist embodied Elijah’s spirit (see {{Malachi 4:5|Malachi 4:5}}; {{Matthew 11:14|Matthew 11:14}}; {{Luke 1:17|Luke 1:17}}; {{John 1:21|John 1:21}}). 

- *you saw*: The past tense shows the angel explained this after John’s vision. 

- *it was, and now is no more*: This contrasts with God, *who is and was and is to come* ({{Revelation 1:4|Revelation 1:4}}, {{Revelation 1:8|8}}). 

- *the Abyss*: See study note on Revelation 9:1–12. 

- Unlike God’s people, the people of this world are not in the Book of Life (see {{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15}}). They will be amazed by the beast’s apparent resurrection (see study note on Revelation 17:10–11; see also {{Revelation 13:13-17|13:13–17}}).
This vision's destruction contrasts with the future of God's people in the new heaven and earth (see {{Revelation 21:1-4|Revelation 21:1–4}}).

- The seven heads of the beast symbolize the seven hills where Rome was built (refer to study note on Revelation 16:10–11). 

- *the woman*: See {{Revelation 17:3-6|Revelation 17:3–6}}.

- *Five have fallen*: If these kings represent Roman emperors, and we start counting from the change from a republic to an empire with Augustus, who ruled from 29 BC to AD 14, then the fifth would be Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68, the sixth would be Vespasian, and the seventh would be Titus. The eighth king would be Domitian.

- *that was, and now is not*: Early commentators argued that Domitian embodied Nero’s spirit (see study note on Revelation 17:8). 

- *the other seven*: This seemingly unbeatable ruler was also destined for destruction.

*The ten horns*, which symbolize world kingdoms following the beast, rule together under his guidance. These verses have led to speculation about a ten-nation alliance. People have guessed it could be the client kingdoms of Rome, the states against the Holy Roman Empire, or the European Union. However, these guesses miss the main point: all nations opposing God will be defeated ({{Revelation 17:14|Revelation 17:14}}).

No matter how much power the beast and ten kings gather ({{Revelation 17:11-12|Revelation 17:11–12}}), they cannot win because Jesus is the Lord of all lords (see {{Revelation 19:11-16|19:11–16}}). Those whom God has called and chosen, and who stay faithful, will stand with him as victors.
Although the prostitute controls the masses, she does not win. Instead, the beast hates and kills her. Satan harms even those he uses for evil.

John reminds us that God is in control. God places a plan in the enemy's mind to fulfill his divine purposes (for example, {{Exodus 7:3|Exodus 7:3}}; {{Exodus 35:31-35|35:31–35}}; {{Ezra 7:27|Ezra 7:27}}; {{Romans 9:18|Romans 9:18}}, {{Romans 9:21|21}}).
This angel got his brightness from heaven. The word *glory* usually describes a divine presence.

The angel's powerful taunt song is the first poetic response. Ancient taunt songs mocked a defeated enemy (see {{Isaiah 13:19-22|Isaiah 13:19–22}}; {{Isaiah 34:10-17|34:10–17}}). These taunts describe the fall of Babylon (or Rome; see study note on Revelation 14:8) as a traumatic event for dependent kingdoms and especially for those who had benefited from her wealth. The Goths and Visigoths attacked Rome in the AD 400s, ending the prosperous empire.

An angel announced that Babylon had fallen. This meant that Babylon’s power was destroyed for ever.

God called his people out of Babylon. He didn’t want them to suffer when that place was destroyed. They were set free from a place where sin and evil were celebrated.

John recorded the songs of people who were sad about Babylon being destroyed. This included the groups who had benefited from Babylon. Kings, traders, merchants, sea captains and sailors had all become rich because of Babylon. Yet Babylon’s wealth and power were based on evil practices.

These included taking over other nations, stealing from them and selling human beings as slaves. It included using more goods than they needed. It included killing people and serving false gods.

God’s people were very glad that God destroyed Babylon’s power. An angel threw a millstone into the sea. This action was a sign. It showed that in God’s kingdom there would never be groups or governments like Babylon.
This chapter includes seven poetic responses to the fall of Babylon or Rome (refer to the study note on Revelation 17:5).

*Fallen, fallen is Babylon*: See {{Isaiah 21:9|Isaiah 21:9}}. Once a beautifully dressed woman (see {{Revelation 17:4|Revelation 17:4}}), Babylon (Rome) became a deserted place for demons and unclean birds like vultures (compare {{Isaiah 13:20-22|Isaiah 13:20–22}}; {{Jeremiah 4:23-31|Jeremiah 4:23–31}}; {{Jeremiah 50:39|50:39}}).
Rome took wealth from conquered nations, living in extreme luxury, before facing God's justice.

*you will not share in her sins*: Being connected to the evil city might result in sharing its punishment and even engaging in its sins (see {{Genesis 13:8-13|Genesis 13:8–13}}; {{Genesis 19:1-29|19:1–29}}; compare {{Jeremiah 51:6|Jeremiah 51:6}}, {{Jeremiah 51:45|45}}).
This second poetic response (see study note on Revelation 18:1–24) warns from heaven to escape the doomed city.

*God has remembered*: His response may seem slow ({{Psalm 103:8|Psalm 103:8}}; {{Psalm 145:8|145:8}}; {{Joel 2:13|Joel 2:13}}; {{Jonah 4:2|Jonah 4:2}}), but God is not weak. He does not forget good or evil ({{Revelation 16:19|Revelation 16:19}}; {{Genesis 19:29|Genesis 19:29}}; {{1 Samuel 1:19|1 Samuel 1:19}}).

*pay her back double*: Some sins were so severe that they required double repayment (see {{Exodus 22:4|Exodus 22:4}}, {{Exodus 22:7|7}}, {{Exodus 22:9|9}}; compare {{Isaiah 40:2|Isaiah 40:2}}; {{Jeremiah 16:18|Jeremiah 16:18}}; {{Jeremiah 17:18|17:18}}).
The plagues ({{Revelation 18:2-3|Revelation 18:2–3}}) remind us that destruction was not just a human action. The Lord God judges her. He is mighty and able to do what he promises.
The kings of the world mourn the loss of the luxury they gained from their alliance with the wicked city.
These three laments show the sadness of those who gained the most from the sinful city's wealthy lifestyle (compare {{Ezekiel 27:1-36|Ezekiel 27}}).
The kings, feeling scared and abandoned (see {{Revelation 18:15|Revelation 18:15}}, {{Revelation 18:17|17}}), stand far away, trying in vain to escape punishment.

The merchants of the world sing the second lament ({{Revelation 18:14|Revelation 18:14}}; see study note on Revelation 18:9–19). They made money from the Roman economy ({{Revelation 18:12-13|Revelation 18:12–13}}), but their trade stopped when the great city was quickly destroyed.

This cargo list shows how much wealth Rome took from its empire (compare {{Ezekiel 27:12-24|Ezekiel 27:12–24}}). It mentions some of the most expensive products of the ancient world, criticizing excessive materialism and pride.
*bodies*: Rome had a large slave market, with historians estimating slaves made up nearly 20% of the population.
The merchants would mourn the fall of Rome (see study note on Revelation 18:1–3) because it would permanently end their usual luxuries. Material goods can disappear in an instant.

*every shipmaster*: Seafarers sing the third lament (see study note on Revelation 18:9–19). They mourn the breakdown of communication and transportation. During Julius Caesar's reign, the Mediterranean was cleared of pirates, and trade flourished under Roman law enforcement. The quick loss of Roman authority would disrupt the trade system.

The laments ({{Revelation 18:9-19|Revelation 18:9–19}}) prompt a call for heaven to rejoice. The people of God should not grieve because the judgment was for them. They had suffered persecution from the evil forces symbolized by the great city.

*a stone the size of a great millstone*: People used heavy millstones, shaped for grinding olives or grain, throughout the ancient world. Jesus also mentioned using such stones for judgment (see {{Matthew 18:6|Matthew 18:6}}). The dramatically thrown boulder symbolized that Rome's power was permanently destroyed.
The songs about Babylon's fall ({{Revelation 18:1-24|Revelation 18:1–24}}) end with a description of the city's destruction.
This scene emphasizes what John heard instead of what he saw. A large crowd offers the first three-part praise (compare {{Revelation 7:9-10|Revelation 7:9–10}}).

In John’s vision, everyone in heaven celebrated that God had judged Babylon and destroyed it. The crowd that John had seen in Revelation chapter 7 shouted Hallelujah! In the Hebrew language hallelujah means praise the Lord.

The smoke that rose from Babylon being burnt never stopped. This was a picture of complete and final judgement. After that, people never had to be afraid of any power like Babylon ever again. This was because God had begun to rule as King over everything.

The crowd sang about the marriage between the Lamb and his bride. The wedding feast was a sign of God’s kingdom coming to earth. In Matthew 22:1–14 Jesus had described himself as the groom in that feast. The bride is a sign for Jesus’ followers and the church.

The Lamb’s bride was the opposite of how John had described Babylon. The bride’s good works and holy living were seen by all.

John was so excited about the wedding feast that he worshipped the angel who announced it. But the angel was a faithful servant of God. He reminded John to worship only God.

This section expands on the message of the sixth song of response ({{Revelation 18:20|Revelation 18:20}}; see study note on Revelation 18:1–24), which called for rejoicing. Various groups offer praises to the Lord. The praises can be divided into two sections: 

- thankfulness for the destruction of evildoers ({{Revelation 19:1-4|Revelation 19:1–4}}) and

- thankfulness for the reward of God’s people ({{Revelation 19:5-8|19:5–8}}).

*true and just* (see {{Revelation 15:3|Revelation 15:3}}; {{Revelation 16:7|16:7}}): In his righteous justice, God fulfilled his promise to judge the great prostitute, who symbolizes moral and spiritual corruption and the persecution of God's people.
*Her smoke*: God's people praise him again when they see the fall of the evil city (compare {{Revelation 14:11|Revelation 14:11}}).

- In response to the first two praises ({{Revelation 19:1-3|Revelation 19:1–3}}), the elders and the living beings (see {{Revelation 4:1-11|Revelation 4}}) again bow before God on the throne (see {{Revelation 4:10|Revelation 4:10}}; {{Revelation 5:8|5:8}}, {{Revelation 5:14|14}}; {{Revelation 7:11|7:11}}). 

- *Amen*: See study note on Revelation 5:14.

The final loud *Hallelujah* emphasizes that God rules as the all-powerful being (see {{Revelation 1:8|Revelation 1:8}}; {{Revelation 4:8|4:8}}; {{Revelation 11:17|11:17}}; {{Revelation 15:3|15:3}}; {{Revelation 16:7|16:7}}, {{Revelation 16:14|14}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}; {{Revelation 21:22|21:22}}).

*For the marriage of the Lamb*: This event, the wedding of the Messiah with his bride, the church (see {{Isaiah 54:5|Isaiah 54:5}}; {{Isaiah 61:10|61:10}}; {{Jeremiah 31:32|Jeremiah 31:32}}; {{Ezekiel 16:7-14|Ezekiel 16:7–14}}; {{Hosea 2:16-20|Hosea 2:16–20}}; {{Mark 2:19-20|Mark 2:19–20}}; {{2 Corinthians 11:2|2 Corinthians 11:2}}), symbolizes complete victory and eternal fellowship.

- *fine linen*: See study note on Revelation 15:5–6.

- *the righteous acts of the saints*: See {{Ephesians 2:8-10|Ephesians 2:8–10}}; {{2 Timothy 3:16-17|2 Timothy 3:16–17}}; {{James 2:18-22|James 2:18–22}}.

- *Blessed are those*: This fourth blessing in Revelation (see {{Revelation 1:3|Revelation 1:3}}; {{Revelation 14:13|14:13}}; {{Revelation 16:15|16:15}}) confirms the hope of the faithful. 

- *who are invited*: God decides who will join.

- *marriage supper* (compare {{Revelation 19:17|Revelation 19:17}}): Jesus often used meals to explain the kingdom ({{Matthew 22:1-13|Matthew 22:1–13}}; {{Luke 14:7-24|Luke 14:7–24}}), and he established a meal for the church ({{Mark 14:22-25|Mark 14:22–25}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:23-26|1 Corinthians 11:23–26}}). 

- *These are true words*: This promise guarantees the message is trustworthy.
The angel gives a strong warning against worshiping the wrong things (compare {{Revelation 22:8-9|Revelation 22:8–9}}).

The rider serves as both a judge and a righteous warrior (see {{Isaiah 11:1-5|Isaiah 11:1–5}}). He is called *Faithful and True*, representing God's authenticity and reliability (see {{Revelation 19:2|Revelation 19:2}}; {{Revelation 21:5-6|21:5–6}}).

*Then I saw*: John describes a new vision of Jesus Christ as a holy warrior and conquering king (see {{Revelation 14:1|Revelation 14:1}}; see also {{Exodus 15:1-7|Exodus 15:1–7}}; {{Psalm 24:8|Psalms 24:8}}; {{Psalm 78:49-50|78:49–50}}; {{Isaiah 59:16-17|Isaiah 59:16–17}}).

John continued seeing more about what had happened before God’s judgement was finished in Revelation 16:17.

Jesus stopped the power of the beast, the false prophet and all who followed them. John described this like a battle. The battle was different from how wars were usually fought in John’s time.

Before the battle, Jesus’ robe was already dipped in blood. This was a sign of how his victory came through his sacrifice on the cross.

Jesus’ army wore clean and fine linen like the Lamb’s bride did in Revelation 19:8. This showed that they shared in Jesus’ victory by following his example for living.

Jesus’ only weapon was the sword from his mouth. Speaking the truth about God was how he stopped his enemies. Everyone who opposed Jesus was destroyed.

The drama reaches its peak: God's enemies face defeat and punishment in two episodes ({{Revelation 19:11-21|Revelation 19:11–21}}; {{Revelation 20:7-10|20:7–10}}). Meanwhile, the faithful enjoy a 1,000-year resurrection ({{Revelation 20:1-6|Revelation 20:1–6}}) followed by the final judgment ({{Revelation 20:11-15|20:11–15}}).

- *He has eyes like blazing fire*: See {{Revelation 1:14-16|Revelation 1:14–16}}; {{Daniel 10:6|Daniel 10:6}}. 

- Christ, wearing many crowns, contrasts with the dragon, whose seven heads each had a crown (see {{Revelation 12:3|Revelation 12:3}}).

- *He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood*: This may refer to: 

- the blood of Christ’s enemies, showing his complete victory ({{Isaiah 63:2-4|Isaiah 63:2–4}}); or

- Christ’s sacrificial death for humanity ({{Revelation 1:7|Revelation 1:7}}). 

- *The Word of God* is John's unique name for Jesus (see {{John 1:1|John 1:1}}, {{John 1:14|14}}).

Christ’s heavenly armies, dressed in victorious white and riding on white horses, contrast with: 

- the locust forces from the abyss ({{Revelation 9:3-11|Revelation 9:3–11}}),

- the three frog-like evil spirits ({{Revelation 16:13|Revelation 16:13}}), and

- the defeated armies at Armageddon ({{Revelation 16:16|Revelation 16:16}}; see also {{Revelation 19:19|19:19}}).

- *from His mouth … a sharp sword*: See {{Revelation 1:16|Revelation 1:16}}; {{Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12}}; see also {{Isaiah 49:2|Isaiah 49:2}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:8|2 Thessalonians 2:8}}. 

- The iron rod symbolizes Christ’s power as ruler and supreme shepherd (see {{Psalm 2:9|Psalms 2:9}}; {{Psalm 23:4|23:4}}). 

- *God the Almighty*: See {{Revelation 1:8|Revelation 1:8}}; {{Revelation 4:8|4:8}}; {{Revelation 11:17|11:17}}; {{Revelation 16:7|16:7}}, {{Revelation 16:14|14}}; {{Revelation 21:22|21:22}}. 

- His fierce wrath will crush his enemies like grapes in a winepress ({{Isaiah 63:2-4|Isaiah 63:2–4}}).

*gather together for the great supper*: This feast on the flesh of the armies fighting against Christ contrasts with the *marriage of the Lamb* ({{Revelation 19:7|Revelation 19:7}}). The enemies ready for battle are quickly destroyed ({{Revelation 19:20-21|Revelation 19:20–21}}; see also {{Revelation 14:17-20|14:17–20}}; {{Revelation 16:16-21|16:16–21}}). Two feasts (the marriage supper of the Lamb in {{Revelation 19:7-8|Revelation 19:7–8}} and the "great supper" of God's judgment in {{Revelation 19:17-18|Revelation 19:17–18}}, {{Revelation 19:21|21}}) offer two views on the end of time. They show the two sides of the good news: 

- grace and judgment, and

- reward and punishment (compare {{John 3:16-18|John 3:16–18}}).

- *the beast … the false prophet*: See {{Revelation 13:1-10|Revelation 13:1–10}}. 

- The fiery lake of burning sulfur symbolizes eternal punishment (see {{Revelation 20:10|Revelation 20:10}}, {{Revelation 20:14-15|14–15}}; {{Revelation 21:8|21:8}}; see also {{Isaiah 66:24|Isaiah 66:24}}; {{Matthew 13:41|Matthew 13:41}}, {{Matthew 13:49-50|49–50}}; {{Mark 9:43|Mark 9:43}}, {{Mark 9:48|48}}). 

- God’s enemies are thrown into the *fiery lake.* The two beasts ({{Revelation 19:20|Revelation 19:20}}) are followed by the dragon ({{Revelation 20:10|20:10}}) and then by death ({{Revelation 20:14|20:14}}) and unsaved humans ({{Revelation 20:15|20:15}}).

The entire enemy army is defeated by the sword from Christ’s mouth (see {{Revelation 1:16|Revelation 1:16}}; {{Revelation 2:12|2:12}}, {{Revelation 2:16|16}}; see also {{Isaiah 11:4|Isaiah 11:4}}; {{Isaiah 49:2|49:2}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:8|2 Thessalonians 2:8}}). One side of God’s word (grace) leads to repentance, while the other side (judgment) delivers the death sentence.

Like the Old Testament *angel of the LORD* (see {{Genesis 16:7-11|Genesis 16:7–11}}; {{Genesis 22:15|22:15}}; {{Exodus 3:2|Exodus 3:2}}; {{Numbers 22:22-34|Numbers 22:22–34}}; {{Judges 2:1-4|Judges 2:1–4}}; {{Judges 6:11-22|6:11–22}}), the angel coming down from heaven has God's authority. This is symbolized by the key that controls the bottomless pit and the power to chain God's great enemy (see {{Revelation 12:7-9|Revelation 12:7–9}}) for a thousand years. 

See the "The Thousand Years (The Millennium)" Theme Note.

This passage has three parts: 

- the binding of Satan ({{Revelation 20:1-3|Revelation 20:1–3}}),

- the reign of God’s holy people ({{Revelation 20:4-6|Revelation 20:4–6}}), and

- Satan's release for a final battle attempt ({{Revelation 20:7-10|Revelation 20:7–10}}).

Four themes emerge: 

- Satan's war is pointless—he cannot resist even an angel;

- God’s holy people will be justified and honored;

- God will achieve the final victory; and

- even when sinful people experience Christ’s good purposes, they still follow Satan when he gains some freedom to act.

In the vision, John saw the end of Satan and of all evil. Satan is another name for the devil.

First, an angel locked the devil in the Abyss for 1,000 years. Then the devil tried again to oppose God. John saw this take place as a battle that the devil organised. He told lies everywhere on earth and convinced the nations to oppose God and God’s people.

John didn’t record a battle. Instead, God sent fire. This stopped those who wanted to destroy God’s plans and his people. Then the devil was thrown into the lake of fire. This was the judgement of second death. That’s how John described the way that God destroyed the devil’s power for ever.

The same thing happened to Death and Hell. After God’s judgement against the devil was completed, God judged all human beings. This was judgement day and the day of the Lord. God’s people had been waiting for it for a very long time.

John saw that every person who had ever lived was judged. Some people had refused to worship the true God and instead worshipped the beast. They weren’t recorded in the book of life. Instead of enjoying God’s kingdom they joined the beast in the lake of fire.

- This imprisonment, described as a bottomless pit (*Abyss*), represents an initial defeat for Satan and the forces of evil. Various New Testament passages explain how Christ's work impacts Satan ({{Luke 10:17-20|Luke 10:17–20}}; {{Acts 10:38|Acts 10:38}}; {{Acts 26:18|26:18}}; {{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}; {{Ephesians 6:11|Ephesians 6:11}}; {{James 4:7|James 4:7}}; see {{Matthew 12:24|Matthew 12:24}}; {{Matthew 16:19|16:19}}; {{Matthew 18:18|18:18}}; {{John 12:31|John 12:31}}; {{1 John 3:8|1 John 3:8}}). Christ's presence with his followers restrains evil powers (see {{2 Thessalonians 2:7|2 Thessalonians 2:7}}), reminding persecuted Christians that they have a future with God. 

- *he could not deceive*: Deception is the devil's hallmark, as he is a liar (see {{John 8:44|John 8:44}}; {{1 John 3:8|1 John 3:8}}); no liar will enter heaven ({{Revelation 21:8|Revelation 21:8}}, {{Revelation 21:27|27}}; {{Revelation 22:15|22:15}}). Faithful believers who experience Christ's reign will not be deceived. 

- The *brief period of time* might symbolize the three and a half years (see {{Revelation 11:2-3|Revelation 11:2–3}}, {{Revelation 11:9-11|9–11}}; {{Revelation 12:14|12:14}}; {{Revelation 13:5|13:5}})—it is a limited time.

- *thrones, and those seated on them*: This image of a heavenly court includes the elders ({{Revelation 4:4|Revelation 4:4}}) on thrones (see {{Daniel 7:9-10|Daniel 7:9–10}}), the victorious martyrs (see {{Daniel 7:22|Daniel 7:22}}), and all of God's people. 

- *beheaded for … Jesus*: Beheading was a common execution method for Roman citizens. 

- The faithful who refused the mark of the beast ({{Revelation 13:16-17|Revelation 13:16–17}}) will judge the condemned (see {{1 Corinthians 6:2-3|1 Corinthians 6:2–3}}) on thrones like those of the worshiping elders (see {{Revelation 4:10-11|Revelation 4:10–11}}; {{Revelation 5:8-10|5:8–10}}; {{Revelation 11:16|11:16}}).
John compares the first resurrection with the second death (see {{Revelation 20:12-15|Revelation 20:12–15}}; compare {{John 5:29|John 5:29}}).

*Blessed*: This fifth blessing in Revelation (see also {{Revelation 1:3|Revelation 1:3}}; {{Revelation 14:13|14:13}}; {{Revelation 16:15|16:15}}; {{Revelation 19:9|19:9}}; {{Revelation 22:7|22:7}}, {{Revelation 22:14|14}}) highlights the promised reward of life. God's faithful people ({{Revelation 20:4|Revelation 20:4}}) will reign with Christ as priests of God (see also {{Revelation 1:6|1:6}}; {{Revelation 5:10|5:10}}).

When Satan is free to act ({{Revelation 20:7|Revelation 20:7}}), he still tries to deceive. He will gather a large army (compare {{Ezekiel 38:1-39:29|Ezekiel 38–39}}) in a final attempt to defeat God's people ({{Revelation 20:9|Revelation 20:9}}).

Satan's attempt to defeat God's people ends with his fiery destruction. This passage has two main purposes: 

- to demonstrate God's complete justice, as Satan and his followers deserve punishment and will not change; and

- to highlight the corruption of those who follow Satan. Even after witnessing Christ's rule for many years, they still join Satan when he is released. 

These reasons form the basis for the judgment at the great white throne ({{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15}}).

- Jewish traditions differ on where Gog and Magog are located. Symbolically, they are to the north (see {{Jeremiah 1:14-15|Jeremiah 1:14–15}}), the direction from which enemies traditionally approached Megiddo and Jerusalem. The names represent nations and rulers from all over the earth that oppose God's people (see {{Ezekiel 38:1-39:29|Ezekiel 38–39}}). 

- *to assemble them for battle*: This repeats earlier scenes where God's enemies gather for battle ({{Revelation 16:16|Revelation 16:16}}; {{Revelation 19:19|19:19}}). Here, Satan makes a final attempt to confront God and his forces.

No battle happens (see {{Revelation 16:16-21|Revelation 16:16–21}}; {{Revelation 19:19-21|19:19–21}}) because fire from heaven comes down and consumes them, just like in Sodom ({{Genesis 19:24|Genesis 19:24}}; see also {{2 Kings 1:10-12|2 Kings 1:10–12}}; {{Ezekiel 38:22-23|Ezekiel 38:22–23}}; {{Ezekiel 39:6|39:6}}). God's enemies cannot stand against him.

*They will be tormented … forever*: Rebellion against God has eternal consequences. Some find the idea of endless punishment disturbing, but Revelation and Scripture generally convey that God will deal strictly with sin and rebellion by those who reject Christ's saving work (see {{Matthew 13:42|Matthew 13:42}}; {{Matthew 25:41-46|25:41–46}}; {{John 3:18|John 3:18}}, {{John 3:36|36}}; {{Romans 2:7|Romans 2:7}}). 

More than any other book in Scripture, Revelation shows that the unrepentant continue their rebellion despite the consequences ({{Revelation 9:20-21|Revelation 9:20–21}}; {{Revelation 16:9-11|16:9–11}}; compare {{Luke 16:31|Luke 16:31}}). Revelation also highlights that God is just and deals with sin as it deserves.
This segment describes a court hearing where the dead are judged based on their actions. God responds to ongoing rebellion with eternal punishment.

- *books were opened*: See {{Psalm 56:8|Psalm 56:8}}; {{Daniel 7:10|Daniel 7:10}}. 

- The *Book of Life* contains the names of faithful people who have experienced God's saving power ({{Malachi 3:16|Malachi 3:16}}; see {{Revelation 3:5|Revelation 3:5}}; {{Revelation 13:8|13:8}}; {{Revelation 17:8|17:8}}; {{Revelation 20:15|20:15}}). They are likely the same ones who experience the *first resurrection* ({{Revelation 20:5-6|Revelation 20:5–6}}).

- *the dead were judged:* The works of both the redeemed and the unredeemed will be judged (see {{Revelation 22:12|Revelation 22:12}}; {{Matthew 16:27|Matthew 16:27}}; {{Matthew 25:31-46|25:31–46}}).

- The phrase *Death and Hades* refers to the reality of death, which is the last enemy God will destroy (see {{Revelation 21:4|Revelation 21:4}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:26|1 Corinthians 15:26}}). 

- The lake of fire represents the terrible end for God's enemies who will not experience the *first resurrection* (see {{Revelation 20:5-6|Revelation 20:5–6}}; compare {{Matthew 25:41|Matthew 25:41}}; {{Luke 16:24|Luke 16:24}}; {{Jude 7|Jude 1:7}}).

- The vision describes God's creation of a new heaven and earth (compare {{Genesis 1:1|Genesis 1:1}} with {{Isaiah 65:17|Isaiah 65:17}}; {{Isaiah 66:22|66:22}}). The old creation has vanished because it was subject to decay (see {{Romans 8:20-21|Romans 8:20–21}}; {{2 Peter 3:7|2 Peter 3:7}}, {{2 Peter 3:10|10}}). 

- *the sea was no more*: The sea symbolized chaos or the abyss (see study note on Revelation 9:1–12) and was sometimes depicted as a roaring monster (see {{Psalm 46:3|Psalms 46:3}}; {{Psalm 74:14|74:14}}; see also {{Job 3:8|Job 3:8}}; {{Job 41:1-34|41:1–34}}; {{Luke 21:25|Luke 21:25}}). The new creation will be free from all such evil.

In the vision, John saw things that Isaiah and other writers in the Bible had talked about. He saw God make heaven and earth new. The world was no longer the way it had been before. There was no sadness, pain or death. This was because God had destroyed sin, death and all evil.

God lived fully with people in what John called the Holy City. John also called it the new Jerusalem. John had seen it come down from heaven. This showed that heaven and earth were made one.

God the Father was the one sitting on the throne. He spoke to John. This hadn’t happened before in the visions. It showed that John could boldly approach God’s throne. The writer of Hebrews had talked about this in Hebrews 4:16. God’s words and promises to his people were tender. His children were safe from all those who had caused harm by their evil deeds.

- *coming down … from God*: The new creation is a gift from God. At first, God created everything good. In the end, God will create a new, perfect world. 

- This image of Jerusalem as a beautiful bride (see {{Isaiah 61:10|Isaiah 61:10}}) contrasts sharply with the vision of Babylon (or Rome) as the prostitute ({{Revelation 17:4-5|Revelation 17:4–5}}; {{Revelation 18:2-3|18:2–3}}; see study note on Revelation 21:9–22:9).

*The dwelling place of God is with man*: The hopes of the Old and New Testaments are fully realized. Since humanity sinned ({{Genesis 3:1-24|Genesis 3}}), separation from God has been humanity's biggest problem ({{Genesis 3:23|Genesis 3:23}}). God has called his people to him through the prophets, Jesus his Son, and the Spirit's presence (see {{Genesis 17:8|Genesis 17:8}}; {{Exodus 29:45-46|Exodus 29:45–46}}; {{Psalm 46:4-5|Psalms 46:4–5}}; {{Psalm 95:7|95:7}}; {{Jeremiah 7:23|Jeremiah 7:23}}; {{Jeremiah 31:33|31:33}}; {{Ezekiel 34:14|Ezekiel 34:14}}; {{Ezekiel 37:27|37:27}}; {{Zechariah 8:8|Zechariah 8:8}}; {{John 14:2-3|John 14:2–3}}; {{John 17:24|17:24}}). In the new heaven and earth, God's people will finally enjoy ultimate and everlasting fellowship with God.

*no more death or mourning or crying or pain*: See {{Isaiah 25:8|Isaiah 25:8}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:54|1 Corinthians 15:54}}. God's people will experience the complete healing and salvation that Christ brings (see {{2 Corinthians 5:17|2 Corinthians 5:17}}; {{Galatians 6:15|Galatians 6:15}}).

- God repeats Jesus’s final words from the cross, *It is done!* ({{John 19:30|John 19:30}}; see also {{Revelation 16:17|Revelation 16:17}}), linking Christ’s death to the promise of eternal life. 

- *I am the Alpha and the Omega*: Using the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, John shows God as the source of all reality and truth. God existed from *the Beginning *(see {{Genesis 1:1|Genesis 1:1}}; see also {{John 1:1-2|John 1:1–2}}) and is also *the End *(see {{Revelation 1:8|Revelation 1:8}}; {{Revelation 22:13|22:13}}). 

- Since Christ is supreme and controls everything (see {{Romans 9:5|Romans 9:5}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:28|1 Corinthians 15:28}}; {{Ephesians 1:22-23|Ephesians 1:22–23}}; {{Ephesians 4:5-6|4:5–6}}), he provides the water of life to all who seek it (see study note on Revelation 7:16–17; see also {{Isaiah 55:1|Isaiah 55:1}}; {{John 4:10|John 4:10}}; {{John 7:37-38|7:37–38}}).

*The one who overcomes*: God's children who persevere in life will receive his blessings. Adoption is a covenant relationship. The language of adoption confirms their privileges and responsibilities (compare {{Genesis 17:8|Genesis 17:8}}; {{2 Samuel 7:14-16|2 Samuel 7:14–16}}; {{Jeremiah 31:33|Jeremiah 31:33}}; {{Ezekiel 34:24|Ezekiel 34:24}}).

- This list summarizes sins described in Revelation. These sins mark those not adopted by God; their fate is the fiery lake (see {{Romans 1:29-32|Romans 1:29–32}}; {{Galatians 5:19-21|Galatians 5:19–21}}; {{2 Timothy 3:2-5|2 Timothy 3:2–5}}; compare {{Exodus 20:13-17|Exodus 20:13–17}}; see also study note on Revelation 20:10). 

- *all liars*: John saw deception as the root of sin; he describes Satan as the *father of lies* elsewhere ({{John 8:44|John 8:44}}; {{1 John 2:4|1 John 2:4}}; see {{Revelation 14:5|Revelation 14:5}}; {{Revelation 21:27|21:27}}; {{Revelation 22:15|22:15}}; compare {{Matthew 12:34|Matthew 12:34}}).

The fourth vision that John wrote about occurred on a huge and high mountain. The vision was of the Holy City of the new heaven and the new earth.

John called this city by several names. He called it Jerusalem and the new Jerusalem. He called it the bride and wife of the Lamb.

This was the city that the writer of Hebrews talked about in Hebrews 11:10 and 16. God had prepared it for those who had faith in him. It was the opposite of the city of Babylon that God had destroyed.

The Holy City was full of God’s glory. John saw this glory through the way the city shone with valuable jewels and gold.

The city was as long as it was high and wide. It had the same shape as the Most Holy Room of the temple. This was a sign of how people could now fully live together with God.

This symbolic vision of the new Jerusalem uses vivid imagery to describe the bride, the wife of the Lamb. It represents all who accept Christ's message of salvation (see {{Revelation 21:2|Revelation 21:2}}; {{Revelation 22:17|22:17}}; {{Ephesians 5:22-32|Ephesians 5:22–32}}).

- *a mountain great and high*: In Scripture, people often experience God on mountains (compare {{Ezekiel 40:2|Ezekiel 40:2}}; see also {{Exodus 3:1|Exodus 3:1}}; {{Exodus 19:10-25|19:10–25}}; {{Deuteronomy 34:1-4|Deuteronomy 34:1–4}}; {{1 Kings 18:20-40|1 Kings 18:20–40}}; {{1 Kings 19:8-18|19:8–18}}; {{Matthew 5:1|Matthew 5:1}}; {{Matthew 15:29|15:29}}; {{Matthew 17:1|17:1}}; {{Matthew 24:3|24:3}}; {{Matthew 28:16|28:16}}). 

- *the holy city … coming down out of heaven from God*: People cannot reach God's presence and eternal life by their own efforts. They receive it as a gift ({{Ephesians 2:8-9|Ephesians 2:8–9}}; compare {{2 Corinthians 5:1|2 Corinthians 5:1}}).

- Like God's true people, the city's glory reflects God's glory (compare {{Exodus 34:29-35|Exodus 34:29–35}}; {{2 Corinthians 3:7-11|2 Corinthians 3:7–11}}). 

- On earth, jasper is not transparent. But in heaven, the jasper is clear like crystal. Its perfect transparency shows God’s purity and integrity (see also {{Revelation 4:3|Revelation 4:3}}; {{Revelation 21:11|21:11}}, {{Revelation 21:18|18}}).

In this vision, the twelve tribes of Israel symbolize God's redeemed people (see {{Revelation 7:4-8|Revelation 7:4–8}}; see also {{Romans 9:6-7|Romans 9:6–7}}). The twelve apostles of the Lamb form the foundation for this community of God's redeemed. Through Jesus, God has fully fulfilled his promise to bless all the families of the earth through Abraham ({{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}).

*measure the city*: Measuring sets accepted boundaries. This contrasts with the unmeasured section of the temple (see {{Revelation 11:2|Revelation 11:2}} and {{Ezekiel 40:3-42:20|Ezekiel 40:3–42:20}}).
The city is a perfect cube. Each side measures 2253 kilometers (Greek *12,000 stadia*). The number *12,000* symbolically represents the people of God (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note).

In the ancient world, walls were important for a city's defense, boundaries, and status. These walls, 65.8 meters thick (Greek *144 cubits*), show the strength of God's redeemed people. The measurement of *144 cubits* uses a multiple of 12 to symbolize God's people. A cubit was the length of a man's forearm, typically about 45.8 centimeters.

The wall is made of jasper (see study note on Revelation 21:11; compare {{Revelation 4:3|Revelation 4:3}}). The city is crafted from gold, which is not opaque like earthly gold. Instead, like God's transformed people, the heavenly gold is clear and pure.

The twelve precious stones on the city's wall foundation remind us of the twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate. These stones represented God's people (see {{Exodus 28:17-20|Exodus 28:17–20}}).
In heaven, common building materials are the things we consider precious and luxurious on earth.

*I saw no temple*: This seems to conflict with earlier visions ({{Revelation 11:19|Revelation 11:19}}; {{Revelation 14:15-17|14:15–17}}). However, each vision in Revelation symbolically represents God's presence. There is no need for a temple in heaven because God is with his people.

In the vision, nothing separated God and the Lamb from God’s people anymore. There was no need for a temple because the entire city was holy.

The purpose of the city’s gates wasn’t to protect the city against attacks. The gates welcomed the kings and nations who came to worship God and the Lamb.

The river John saw was like the river Ezekiel had seen. Ezekiel’s vision was recorded in Ezekiel 47:1–12. The river was the water of life. That is another name for living water. God had offered this water in Revelation 21:6. He would give it for free to anyone who asked for it.

The tree of life grew on both sides of the river. This showed that the city was also a new Garden of Eden. All nations could always eat from the tree of life’s fruit. Eating it brought healing.

The curse was no more. This was the curse talked about in Genesis chapter 3. It was the way that all of creation suffered after human beings sinned. In the new creation, human beings served God and were rulers together with him.

- The city's vitality, energy, and life come from the glory of God and the Lamb, not from institutions or physical sources of power and light. The sun and moon were part of the first creation ({{Genesis 1:14-19|Genesis 1:14–19}}; see {{Isaiah 60:19-20|Isaiah 60:19–20}}).
